#8119. 32 Old-Fashioned Girl Names Pulled Straight Out Of Vintage Cookbooks

These will take you right back to Grandma’s recipe box.

I still remember walking into my grandma’s kitchen, with its scuffed-up parquet floors and antique wooden dining table, and pulling a spiral-bound community cookbook from a makeshift shelf in the corner. Maybe it was the writer in me, but I always loved to leaf through the names of the women who’d put the book together and picture them, like my grandma, sprinkling herbs into a bubbling pot over the stove or putting the finishing touches on a latticed holiday pie. At least for me, a big part of the magic in those books was the bylines. Every dip, casserole, and suspiciously gelatinous salad came with a name attached, and those names were *chef’s kiss.*

I unfortunately have no idea where my grandma’s collection of yellowing community cookbooks went, but thankfully the internet lives forever. I found and flipped through vintage collections published from 1947 to 1988 (from the deep South to a historic church in Hawaii), pulling some of the best first names off the recipe cards. Not surprisingly, many are straight-up coastal-grandma-coded (looking at you, Maude). Others I’d never heard of prior to stumbling upon them.

And how fun that there’s a sweet little origin story to go along with each one? If you name your baby Bea, you can tell people it was inspired by a woman who made very good baked clams in 1983. Charming! So, with further ado, here are 32 vintage baby names straight from old cookbooks.

Inspired by: Josephine Marner’s shrimp cocktail dip, Centennial Cookbook (1979)

I’m a sucker for a name that's easy to shorten, and you can’t ask for an easier one than Josephine: Jo, Josie, even Posey or Fifi work here. Of Hebrew origin, it means “God will increase.”

Inspired by: Ida Gilberg Spitzer’s braided egg twist, Heritage Cookbook (1975)

This short and sturdy name most likely makes you think of Ida B. Wells, a journalist, educator, and early leader in the Civil Rights Movement. And, really, who wouldn’t want a name shared by such an icon? German and Greek in origin, it means “hardworking.”

Inspired by: Thora Hawkins Linebaugh’s butter flake rolls, Heritage Cookbook (1975)

Any ‘90s kid will tell you this name has coolness to spare thanks to Hocus Pocus star Thora Birch. But it’s also the feminine form of Thor, aka a Norse thunder god, which makes it feel a little tough, too.

Inspired by: Maude Lyman’s chicken casserole, West Oakland Soul Food Cookbook (1963)

Thanks to Judd Apatow and Leslie Mann’s daughter, Maude Apatow, this one reads less like a church potluck and more like It Girl these days. A medieval form of Matilda, it means “mighty in battle.”

Inspired by: Viola Taylor’s deep-dish peach pie, West Oakland Soul Food Cookbook (1963)

This name conjures up a lot: Shakespeare’s clever heroine in Twelfth Night, a flower, an instrument, and of course, our queen Viola Davis. Latin, it means “purple flower.”

Inspired by: Rosemary Riglar’s cheese netties, Lula No Ke Kuke Ana Historic Hawaiian Church Cookbook (1983)

Any herb name comes with built-in kitchen cred, and Rosemary happens to be one of the absolute prettiest. Bonus: Rosie, Romy, and Mae are all on the table for nicknames.

Inspired by: Gertie Carey’s fresh lemon cake, West Oakland Soul Food Cookbook (1963)

I can’t be the only one who thinks this name is off-the-charts adorable, can I?! It always makes me think of Drew Barrymore’s character in E.T., which endeared it to an entire generation. The cute short form of Gertrude, it means “spear strength.”

Inspired by: Clarinda Ward’s oatmeal bread, Centennial Cookbook (1979)

A truly unique option, Clarinda is a literary invention built on Clara, which means “bright.” Poet Robert Burns used it as a pen name for the woman he wrote swoony letters with. Romantic-era BookTok vibes!

Inspired by: Estelle Braaf’s Pate “En Croute,” The Good Neighbor’s Cookbook (1983)

I mean, any woman serving pâté en croûte at a neighborhood potluck was clearly the Estelle Getty of her block, y’know? This name serves serious Hollywood glamour with a meaning to match: “star.”

Inspired by: Tibby Ellison Simmons’ fresh mint punch, Heritage Cookbook (1975)

While this is historically an old Scottish nickname for Isabel or Elizabeth, millennials will recognize it as the name of Amber Tamblyn’s character in The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants.

Inspired by: Ione Jones’ baked popped corn, Lula No Ke Kuke Ana Historic Hawaiian Church Cookbook (1983)

Pronounced eye-OH-nee, this Greek name means “violet.” It’s definitely not one you have to worry about five other kids on the playground having, and it’s got a bit of Gen X dreaminess to it thanks to Ione Skye.

Inspired by: Nora Kremers’ Tillamook Bay clam chowder, Tillamook County Bicentennial Cookbook (1976)

Already a modern favorite, this name is traditionally short for Honora or Eleanor. Although if you grew up in the ‘90s, you probably associate it most with Nora Jones or the Blessid Union of Souls song by the same name.

Inspired by: Virgie Dow’s butterhorns, Community Cookbook Order of Eastern Star (1981)

Admittedly, I’m a bit partial to this one; it was my great-grandmother’s name! It’s sweet, Southern, and folksy… just like she was. Of Latin origin, it means “maiden” and would make an excellent nickname for the longer Virginia.

Inspired by: Lenora Buck’s party meatballs, Pine to Prairie Cookbook (1988)

A diminutive of Leonora or Eleanor, this name has a touch of moodiness because it echoes Poe’s “Lenore.” Nora and Lennie are the easy nicknames here, although you could go more gender-neutral with Len or even Leo.

Inspired by: Jetta Meads’ Y-U-M-M-Y cocoa pie, Community Cookbook Order of Eastern Star (1981)

Often a Dutch nickname for Henrietta, Jetta is also derived from the English word for a glossy black gemstone. It has a bit of old-school Hollywood sophistication to it as well, seeing as Jetta Goudal was a prominent Dutch-American silent film actress from the ‘20s.

Need even more inspo? Here are a few more, pulled straight from cookbooks of yore.

#8118. How To Get Fantastic Sleep

Are parents doomed to a lifetime of chasing after good sleep?

On a tip from a savvy movie critic, I took my 7-year-old out to see his second ever Marvel movie the other day (he's a big fan of Norse mythology so he's seen Thor: Ragnarok and sorta liked it). We sat back, donning our 3D glasses (he was very into the novelty of this) and took in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. What a pleasant surprise. The movie is, in fact, as my movie critic colleague promised, The Best Marvel Movie for Families.

For the kids, there’s a lot to love. There are the action montages, a bright retro futuristic setting, a visual style that is gee-whiz superhero cool, but in a comic way — shiny and light and not over the top. The movie is just more palatable for kids than most other Marvel movies, emotionally and cognitively. The superheroes are relatable as family but they also play the part of role models well, interacting with and caring deeply about the public they serve. The villain, too, is not so much motivated by evil but by an unstoppable appetite (for planets, granted) that he is actively trying to rid himself of. A little sympathy goes a long way to take the teeth out of a monster. But most importantly there’s Franklin, the baby.

The Fantastic Four are a family and have arguments and issues that are familiar to all kids. One big one is the strain (and joys) that having a baby puts on, well, everyone. I especially loved seeing Reed Richards and Sue Storm, superheroes with doctorates who no doubt have seen their share of sleep debt, complain about tiredness. Even genius superheroes can’t face the superheroic task that is getting baby to bed. It’s a tension that gets the screen time it deserves. Just ask any parent.

Sleep has been on my mind a lot lately. I always thought that I would crush sleep once my baby grew up, but some 6 years later I realize maybe it wasn’t the baby? I’ve never met someone who doesn’t have a tenuous relationship with sleep. When I was in physical prime either during my senior high school years as a soccer player and middle distant runner or during my marathon-happy thirties, I slept so very soundly. At least that’s how I remember it.

Now that I’m older I juggle more — so much more — work out a little less and do a lot more staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night. With age, I maybe need to admit, I need an assist.

I’ve only just started to give sleep tracking a fair shake. I’ve been pairing up a new Samsung Galaxy 8 watch with a Samsung Galaxy Ring (I’ve been a Samsung man since I converted to their Flip phone, which pairs seamlessly together, requiring no third-party apps).

So what have I found? That data is in fact motivating. I won’t get too into the weeds but I will tell you that late night snacks, screens, night caps, and work are bad for my sleep. Evening walks, reading, and days with lighter fare and more quality workouts lead to more quality sleep.

It’s all fairly obvious stuff, but what the tracking does is force the attention. Good sleep matters and is, for those of us without babies, a fairly controllable thing. We can create habits that help sleep. We can choose to prioritize our health and well being. Stats don’t tell us what to do, but they do show what our current priorities.

When my son was a sleepless baby (he really was the worst) the only two priorities I had were to keep him healthy (alive) and to find sleep. My world is a little easier now and my list of priorities has grown immensely. I want to be outdoors more, to find new fitness, to take on new passions (birding is kind of fun, everyone), to embrace a new phase of marriage, to learn new skills, and meet my kids where they are. But sometimes you have to remember the basics. Without good sleep, everything is more difficult. Only a superhero can defeat the eater of worlds on a new parent’s sleep schedule. The rest of us need all the help we can get.

#8117. The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

How should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have said,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”

My Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”

This resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The New York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”

Bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”

This metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

We’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a big piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

#8116. The Only Time I Felt Allowed To Be Overweight Was When I Was Pregnant

Pregnancy didn't make me comfortable gaining weight. It made my weight explainable.

I'd never gone 24 hours without thinking about my weight. Never a day where I didn’t feel guilty for overeating and what the scale would look like the next morning. Forever overweight and forever ashamed.

Then I got pregnant. I arrived at my new high-risk OB-GYN, the one I had to search for because my BMI alone made me automatically high risk. No preexisting medical conditions, no concerning family history… just FAT. And before I could even wrap my head around the fact that I was growing an actual human being, my new doctor told me that because of my BMI, I should only gain 11 pounds over the next nine months.

I was supposed to grow a whole ass baby, and only gain 11 pounds? Historically, I could gain 11 pounds overnight if I put my mind to it! I thought pregnancy was the one time I could finally embrace getting bigger. I actually envisioned stepping on the scale at the doctor's office without fear, maybe even getting a little golf clap from my doctor for gaining a few pounds. Like the prize pig at the county fair.

I understood there were medical reasons behind the recommendation, but I couldn't help feeling defeated. Here I was, finally experiencing something I had dreamed about, and somehow, the conversation had already come back to my weight. Even when my body was literally supposed to get bigger, there was a limit.

I felt ashamed. And that shame quickly turned into anxiety. I'd spent my entire life fearing weight gain for myself, but now I was terrified it could hurt someone else: my baby. Instead of embracing my growing body, I spent my first trimester afraid of what would happen if it grew too much.

By week 12, stress and morning sickness had caused me to lose 10 pounds. I stepped on the scale at my next ultrasound, secretly excited and doing some quick math. Did that mean I could gain 21 pounds now? Did the math carry over? I was already calculating how to earn more weight gain. But when I spoke with my doctor, he didn't mention the weight loss at all. He wasn't proud, he wasn't mad. Not a peep.

And somehow, this felt like a green light to me. Like actually, maybe he isn’t THAT focused on the scale and more focused on the baby (duh). After that appointment, I felt my jaw unclench, and something in my brain shifted. I had made it through the first trimester, the baby was healthy and I had lost weight. For thatI was not punished nor rewarded. It was finally, just a number.

So I announced my pregnancy to family and friends and a sudden weight was lifted (and soon gained). Eventually, even the morning sickness let up and I reverted back to the old me. And just like that, I was back in my safe space, scrolling DoorDash.

I started eating whatever I wanted and felt no shame. I ate mozzarella sticks for a snack at 10am. Bagels before bed. I would end every meal with a “treat” of Phish Food ice cream or a couple peanut butter cups for good measure. It’s called palate cleansing.

It felt like FREEDOM. I didn't have to suck in my stomach or hide my rolls. No worrying about posing for a picture to make myself look smaller or hide my sins. I didn't have to wonder if someone was looking at what was on my plate, because honestly I DARE YOU. I didn't have to promise myself I'd “be good tomorrow.” My belly was supposed to get bigger. My clothes were supposed to stop fitting. I was supposed to gain weight. It was like a fun topic of conversation with my girlfriends and people who were already moms… “eating myself through house and home, you know how it goes!”

Well, spoiler alert, I saw their 11 pounds and ended up raising them 50. And honestly? I wasn't that scared. I'd been that weight before. I knew what it was like to live in that body. The number I was supposed to fear reaching was a number I'd already seen on my own scale. But more than that, for the first time in my life, my growing body came with an explanation.

The craziest part? My doctor didn’t bring up my weight again until after I had the baby. Sure, it still made the occasional cameo, like when I needed an anesthesia consultation before birth because of my BMI. But it made my weight felt more like a supporting character instead of the entire plot. It felt like a huge relief.

Pregnancy didn't make me comfortable gaining weight. It made my weight explainable. Because the reality is, I didn't suddenly stop being plus-size. For once in my life I felt normal…like maybe this is how regular people go about their day. Like I was in a new tier of women, one where people were going to celebrate my growing belly. My dad would make us dinner on Sundays and say “Mary gets extra, she’s eating for two!” This is what dreams were made of.

Before I knew it, nine months had flown by and I'd given birth to my baby boy. Less than 12 hours postpartum, a visiting doctor looked at my legs and asked, “Do your legs typically look like this, or are you really swollen?”

Nope, that's just what my legs look like. I'd barely had a minute to process giving birth before I was back to feeling self-conscious about my body. Nine months of freedom, gone in one sentence.

And that was just the beginning. Soon, doctor's appointments included questions like, “So, what's your plan for weight loss?” and suggestions about GLP-1 medications. My health was otherwise good, but once again, my weight was the conversation.

I remember thinking, how am I supposed to diet on no sleep? I'm just trying to keep a newborn alive, recover from childbirth, and make it through the day. Could my body just exist for a minute without needing to be fixed?

But still, I felt the pressure to lose weight, like my body was a project that was never finished. I even caught myself feeling relieved on days when I was so busy caring for my baby that I barely had time to eat.

I've spent my entire life trying to make my body smaller, and for most of my pregnancy, I finally got to celebrate getting bigger. I wish I could say that experience changed the way I see myself forever, but the truth is, I still think about my weight every day. I still feel the guilt, still do the mental math, still wonder what the scale will say tomorrow. My brain is programmed this way. But pregnancy gave me a taste of freedom I never knew was missing. For once, I got to exist in my body without feeling like I owed anyone an explanation.

Sometimes I wonder if I will ever feel that free again. After giving birth to two beautiful boys, I don’t long for another pregnancy, though I have to admit, nine more months of not obsessing over the scale sounds pretty damn appealing.

I don’t want another excuse to love my body, I just want to stop feeling like I need one.

Mary Burnham is a plus-size boy mom of two who manages software by day and chaos by night. She’s highly susceptible to a viral product and even more susceptible to self-diagnosing the latest health scare. Virality at all costs. Follow her at @maryuburnham.

#8115. The 10 hottest kids’ Halloween costumes of 2026, according to Google

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 20, 2026

Every October, parents become amateur anthropologists, scouring the internet for a Halloween costume that will satisfy one small, extremely opinionated client. (Or, more likely, researching a request for a character we’ve never heard of.)

Now, Google has put all that frantic searching into one place. Its new site, Frightgeist, tracks which costumes are top ranked in search, and the kids’ top ten for 2026 is a gloriously incoherent collection. We’ve got a country legend we’re still mourning, a Thriller-era King of Pop, a web-cartoon jester, and, with no explanation offered, a dumpling.

There’s no tidy theme to sum it up, and I’ve stopped trying. Here’s what you need to know about this year’s top costumes, along with advice for putting a look together.

It just makes sense that our dearly departed Saint of Tennessee comes in at No 1. And since Dolly sported so many iconic looks across a long parade of eras, you have the opportunity to seem like you’re presenting your child with options even when there’s a solid chance this was your idea, not theirs. The only must is a blonde wig that defies gravity. A stuffed bra is optional but encouraged–Dolly would have wanted it that way.

Makes sense she’s spiking, since she’s leading this year’s CMA nominations with nine nods and “Choosin’ Texas” made her the only woman to top the Hot 100, Hot Country Songs, and Country Airplay charts at once. That said, I’ll be honest. Unless said trick-or-treater is belting out “Choosin’ Texas,” this costume will be lost on me. But any excuse to pile on some rhinestones is a good one. (See above.)

The lone non-celebrity in the lineup and, I’d wager, the only costume on this list your kid actually chose for themselves. Chalk it up to the squishy dumpling toys, the brightly colored, bamboo-steamer-packaged squishies that have been dominating TikTok and every kid’s pocket this year. On the plus side, the costume is cozy, warm, and fully nap-compatible. No notes.

Between her two World Cup performances last summer and the early-2000s revival in full swing, she was overdue. I recently combed the attic for my old low-rise jeans, the ones with the half-inch zipper, because my teenage daughter asked for them in earnest. The horror.

Pokémon turns 30 this year, which makes it officially old enough to have trained a generation of parents before becoming their kids’ obsession. Give them a backwards red cap, tuck a Pikachu they already own under one arm, and you’ve got the cheapest, most comfortable costume on the list. Additionally, they’ll be recognizable to every other kid on the block which, for better or worse, is more than I can say for the country singers above.

The show hit its 20th anniversary this year, which means the early-aughts kids who wore out the DVDs are now the ones doing the costume shopping. And if you need another reason to love the pick, Miley is Dolly’s goddaughter, which makes number one and number six a true family affair.

Worth noting that the lone superhero to crack this entire top ten is a woman who also drums in a punk rock band. That’s the kind of role model I can get behind. Spider-Man? Old news. And there’s no new movie to credit here, which means the kids are picking her on pure merit.

Specifically the Thriller era, so we’re talking red leather jacket and at least a loose attempt at the choreography. If your kid can pull off the zombie shoulder roll, they’ll absolutely crush this one. Credit the Antoine Fuqua biopic, “Michael,” that hit theaters last spring and put the moonwalk back in heavy rotation.

Admittedly, I had to look this one up. Turns out, she’s a jester trapped in a digital circus having a slow-motion existential crisis, which tells you this is for the tween and up set–not the toddlers. If your kid is asking for it, they’re too old for the cute stuff and whether you knew it or not, you’re officially in a new stage of parenting. The hat is non-negotiable, though.

Baby Yoda by any other name, and still the single most efficient way to make a small child look even smaller and more adorable. The ears make it truly irresistible and though your stroller may not float, it can still be part of the costume.

And there you have it. Ten costumes, roughly four decades, and one dumpling. Whoever your child opts into being this year, may the wig defy gravity and the candy be plentiful.

#8114. What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and important meditation about masculinity.

Will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

“I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he said to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

When it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”

Finally, he says that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

Danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

#8113. What Couples Who Survive A Betrayal Do In The First Six Months

These steps apply to more than just cheating.

Your partner is your person, your safe place, your rock — so when they betray you unexpectedly, it can feel like the ground split open beneath you, and there’s no more safety net. Maybe you’re not sure what to do next. Maybe you’re thinking of ending things, or you want to try and work on it first. Whatever happened and wherever you are, there are certain steps couples take after a betrayal that relationship experts say predict whether or not they’ll move forward together or fall apart.

For starters, a betrayal doesn’t just mean someone cheated. Any breach of trust can feel like betrayal, says Blythe Landry, M.Ed., licensed clinical social worker, author of Trauma Intelligence, and founder of Grief to Purpose. Quitting a job without letting your partner know, buying a car or adopting a pet without discussing it first, or parenting in a way your partner is opposed to behind their back — these are all betrayals. So too are having affairs and endangering your kids, like drinking and driving with them in the car, Landry explains.

Those first six months after a betrayal are when the pain is most acute, Landry says. And following any type of betrayal, each partner is going to face their own unique hurdles.

“Oftentimes, the betrayed partner has difficulty determining if things are safe emotionally, as well as being uncertain of what they can believe about their relationship,” Suzanne Koch Eckenrode, licensed marriage and family therapist at Carlsbad Beach Recovery. “The person responsible for breaking the trust may be experiencing feelings of guilt, shame, or defensiveness. One of the biggest obstacles to healing is the fact that both parties will heal at a different rate. It can be very challenging to begin the process of healing when one feels ready to proceed while the other does not feel ready.”

So, how do you begin to move forward at all? Here’s what the experts advise.

Instead of trying to immediately forgive and move on, couples who stick together put their energy toward being consistent with one another, says Koch Eckenrode. This is what rebuilds trust in the long run.

“The couple establishes clear boundaries, communicates in an open manner when they feel uncomfortable or angry, and takes responsibility without blaming the other person,” she says. “Typically, rebuilding a relationship is not achieved by a single grand action but through many actions, to create enough positive interactions so the two people begin to trust each other again gradually.”

In most cases, the “perpetrator” has not suddenly turned evil and betrayed their partner. These things don’t happen in a vacuum.

“There is often a history of communication differences and things that are going on that lead one party to do something,” Landry says. “Now, that does not make the other person responsible for their choice to betray. But for example, if someone is constantly criticized and they are afraid to tell the truth because [of it], they may be much more likely to do something that they don’t tell their partner about. So one very positive sign is if both parties can look at their accountability.”

One partner may feel chronically unheard, rejected, or disrespected, which ultimately leads to a betrayal of some kind, Landry says. While it doesn’t excuse them, it does explain the behavior — and it reveals what needs fixing to move forward in your relationship together.

When a normally good, moral person betrays their partner, typically something inside of them is not OK. Either because they don’t want to or don’t know how to process those feelings, they look for something external to help. Maybe it’s an affair partner because their spouse no longer seems sexually interested in them. Maybe it’s drinking too much because it takes the edge off the bad feelings. But their commitment to understanding their own behavior plays a major role in healing and rebuilding trust.

And, importantly, the other partner is patient while they suss out what led them to stray.

“It’s always easy to see when it’s not you,” Landry says. “That’s what I would say to anyone going to couples counseling or even going to a pastor or whoever you go to for help. When it’s inside of you, it’s so evasive sometimes.”

Thinking back to her own clients, Landry says the couples in which both partners were genuinely invested in fixing things — those were the ones who repaired their relationships. That meant both showing up for counseling, both taking accountability, and both being vulnerable throughout the process.

5. They communicate, communicate, communicate until that becomes the norm.

Let’s say one partner travels often for work, and has also used that time to gamble away large sums of money in secret before. Short of quitting that job and never traveling again, how can the couple handle this scenario in a way that rebuilds trust?

“Discuss your travels beforehand and establish reasonable times for checking in with one another, then immediately inform each other of any changes from the plan,” says Koch Eckenrode. “The person doing the travel will be expected to follow through and do as agreed upon without having to constantly be reminded. The purpose here is not to provide some sort of long-term surveillance system; it’s to create an environment where each person feels safe enough that they are transparent about their actions naturally because it has become a part of who they are as opposed to being something they need to do.”

If you had good communication before the betrayal, that’s usually the biggest indicator that you two will successfully get through this as a couple, Landry says.

This has more to do with your personalities than the relationship itself, Landry notes, but the ability to see each other in a positive light will get you far. When the betrayed party has the capacity to look at their partner and say, “This is a good person who did a bad thing,” that’s a really good sign.

Of course, there are those people who don’t deserve this level of grace. “There’s a difference between giving someone another chance and holding them in high regard and letting someone abuse you. Make sure that you’re not so attached to someone that they’ve done something repeatedly to betray you and you’re holding onto it in the name of compassion, and really you’re harming yourself,” she says.

Again, it’s impossible to see yourself and your behaviors clearly all the time, Landry says. This is where the support of a therapist, family member, religious leader, or other non-biased third party can be helpful.

“Before you go to a professional, make sure to ask them questions like, ‘What have you done before? Have you worked with other couples in this situation? Do you work on yourself?’ I have never had a pre-client ask me if I go to therapy, but I really wish they would because you really shouldn’t be helping people unless you're helping yourself,” Landry says.

If you do opt to lean on a pastor or church elder for guidance, make sure they are not going to encourage you to stay in an unhealthy relationship, she adds. “The cool thing about therapy is that the therapist will have to see each of you individually prior to doing couples counseling. And they are doing that to make sure the relationship is safe.”

The season may be winding down but there’s plenty you can do now to protect those tubers so your dahlias come back stronger next summer. These 5 secrets unlock your best blooms ever

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first fall frosts bring a dramatic and abrupt curtain call to flower borders. And for any dahlias that might have been bursting with dinner-plate blooms just days earlier, it can come as a bit of a shock when freezing temperatures leave them limp and shriveled. For new dahlia growers, this sudden collapse can be devastating. Yet while the stems and leaves may be wilting and the flowers may be done, the tubers remain very much alive and capable of producing decades of future blooms.

So take heart, because you can enjoy those gorgeous displays again, as long as you take the right steps now. The days following first frosts are critical if these tubers are to push new growth out next year. These Mexican and Central American natives need care in order to see out the next few months. If these tubers are subjected to hard-frozen subsoil or waterlogged winter mud, they might easily rot and perish.

To keep your favorite cultivars thriving year after year, you need to decide how to overwinter dahlias, either by lifting the tubers for indoor storage or by applying the right protection and insulation in milder regions. The right approach depends on your regional hardiness zone, local soil drainage, and weather. While it might be a little daunting at first, getting your dahlias ready for winter is a relatively simple process. Whether you lift or leave in the ground, here’s how to prime your dahlias for winter.

Timing is key if you want your dahlia tubers to survive winter, and it’s vital to pay heed to your USDA hardiness zone to help your dahlia tubers to survive winter. Never dig your dahlias before the initial frost. That frost sends a biochemical signal through the plant, letting it know that the growing season has ended. In response, the plant channels its remaining energy down into the ground, plumping up the tubers in preparation for dormancy. So allowing the blackened stems to rest untouched for a week or so after this frost ensures the tubers reach peak maturity.

Your overwintering choices will depend on where you live. If you are in zones 6 and colder, it’s best to lift tubers every fall. Winter ground freezes in these latitudes can be lethal for unprotected tubers. Zone 7 gardens are borderline: lifting is still advised, but tubers in sandy, well-draining soil can survive beneath heavy insulation. In mild southern and coastal regions (zones 8-11), many dahlia varieties can remain safely in the ground, provided winter soil drains freely and the tubers have some protection.

You don’t have to remove the tubers right after the first frost. Let the foliage die back naturally. Any green foliage is still collecting energy to store in the tubers. You don’t want to disrupt that process prematurely. However, if you are in a very cold climate where the ground is going to freeze before the foliage has died, don’t wait. Keep an eye on the weather forecast to decide when to dig and lift your tubers. The goal is to let them mature without freezing them. In warmer climates, you have more flexibility.

Before you start, check the soil with a soil meter like the Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter from Amazon. This will help you determine when the ground is nearing that freezing threshold ahead of lifting or mulching. Dahlia type and variety matter, too. Massive dinner plate varieties (such as Café au Lait) produce heavy tuber clumps that require longer drying times, whereas compact varieties (like the Gallery series) form tight root balls that dry quickly. Whichever area and variety you have, these steps will help you to ensure your dahlias return with a bang next summer…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The first step is to cut back stems and foliage. Once the foliage has blackened and you have allowed the root system a week to absorb its final starches, you’re ready. Using sharp bypass pruners, sever the main stalks down to 4-6 inches (10-15cm). If you are after a pair of bypass pruners, the Corona BP Dual Link Bypass Pruners from Amazon are perfect for slicing through the thick stalks in a single pass without crushing vital tissue.

Leaving short, sturdy stems is vital, as it gives you a safe gripping point for lifting the heavy tuber clusters and reduces pressure on delicate tuber necks. You can also use them to attach identifying labels. Just make sure that you cut the stalks just before lifting. Dahlia stalks are hollow, so if you cut stems down and leave them through days of heavy rain, water will pool around the tuber and trigger rot. Cut on a dry morning and plan to lift tubers the same day to keep water from causing problems.

Now, you’re ready to lift your tubers, but do it slowly and carefully. The tuberous roots and the narrow neck that connects them to the crown can break easily. If these necks snap, twist, or crack during digging, the tuber becomes useless. Use a garden fork to dig several inches around the plant. Get under the roots with the fork, inserting the tines 10-12 inches (25-30cm) away from the main stem. Rock the fork handle backward to loosen the soil, working in a full circle around the plant.

Gently lift the clump, using the shortened stems to help, but don’t yank hard on the stalk. Once lifted, gently shake away loose clods of earth. Inspect the roots, and snip away any soft, mushy, or damaged tubers. However, resist dividing the tubers now. Those cuts can leave them vulnerable to rot or infections in winter storage. You can add a little sulfur power such as Bonide Sulfur Plant Fungicide Dust from Walmart to stems to prevent storage rots. Alternatively, dust stem cuts with a little cinnamon.

Your tubers will need a little time to dry before being packed away. Place them upside down on slatted wooden trays, wire screens, or newspaper in a shaded, frost-free, well-ventilated space at 55-65°F (13-18°C). Let the clumps dry for 2-3 days until the skin feels dry and leathery. But don’t leave them so long that the tubers begin to wrinkle or shrivel.

Pack the dry tubers in breathable containers, such as cardboard boxes, wooden apple crates, or plastic storage totes with the lids cracked open. Nestle the tubers in a sterile, moisture-buffering medium, such as dry vermiculite, horticultural perlite, coarse wood shavings, or peat-free coir. You can buy Miracle-Gro Perlite from The Home Depot to help cushion dormant tubers while absorbing excess humidity to prevent winter mold. Make sure individual tubers do not touch.

Move your container into a dark, unheated room, such as a cellar, basement corner, or frost-free garage. Make sure it holds steady at 40-50°F (4-10°C). Stored tubers need a balance of moisture and dryness. Check on the tubers a few times over winter. If they are too moist, repack in drier material. If too dry, give them a light spritz of water.

If you are in zones 8-11 (or a sheltered microclimate in zone 7), you can overwinter your dahlia tubers in the ground. However, success depends on 3 factors: mild winters, excellent winter soil drainage, and insulation. Heavy clay soil that stays saturated in winter will rot tubers in the ground, regardless of ambient air warmth. Wait for the first frost to blacken the leaves, then cut the stalks down to 2-3 inches (5-8cm). Immediately cap the hollow stem ends with small inverted plastic cups, foil wraps, or a dab of horticultural wax to prevent rain from channeling into the crowns.

After cutting back dead stems, spread a generous 4-6-inch (10-15cm) blanket of loose, organic mulch over the surface. Try team favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Mulch from Amazon for a lush bark mulch that insulates from freeze-thaw cycles and suppresses weeds. You can also use clean agricultural straw or chopped dry leaves for protection against cold snaps, while helping to maintain healthy soil aeration.

Container-grown dahlias are vulnerable to freeze-thaw shocks. Left on an exposed patio, tubers can turn to ice in hours, while ceramic and terracotta planters are prone to cracking. It’s wise to move the container to a sheltered location for winter. Just be sure the soil will stay dry and the storage area won’t freeze. Once frost kills foliage, cut the stalks back to 4 inches (10cm), cease watering, and allow the potting mix to dry out. In colder regions, move the pot to an unheated garage, shed, or basement where temperatures are 35-45°F (2-7°C). If indoor space is unavailable in borderline zones, cluster containers tightly against a sheltered, south-facing foundation wall.

Wrap the containers in heavy layers of burlap or thermal bubble wrap, and mound loose straw over the top of the soil as a light mulch layer. Sta-Green Burlap Blankets from Lowe’s are a great breathable option for insulating grouped containers against winter winds and chills. Alternatively, you can lift and store tubers, just as with in-ground dahlias. Unpot the root ball, gently tease away the potting mix, and store the bare tubers in crates of vermiculite, just as you would for in-ground tubers.

Just because this season is over, that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy your dahlias again. A little extra effort now allows you to enjoy these gorgeous blooms year after year. Caring for your dahlias after the first fall frosts doesn’t require special techniques or time-intensive labor. A half hour is all you need to cut back frost-nipped stalks, lever tuber clumps from the earth, and pack them into cozy quarters, or protect them if you leave them where they are. If you do tuck your tubers away this month, you just need to check in on them occasionally over winter Next year, your tubers will be in great shape and fully primed to deliver your most breathtaking blooms yet.

#8111. Are Our Chidlren Really So Mentally Unwell?

American kids are having a mental health crisis like no other. What are we to do with all these diagnoses?

In a New York Time ideas story that ran this past week, Jia Lynn Yang opens with a bang: “One of the more bewildering aspects of the already high-stress endeavor of 21st-century American parenting is that at some point your child is likely to be identified with a psychiatric diagnosis of one kind or another. Many exist in a gray zone that previous generations of parents never encountered.”

For those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious. For those with younger ones, buckle up.

In Yang’s story, she focuses on the role schools play. Failures in education may lead to an increase of psychiatric diagnoses like ADHD — alongside IEPs or maybe medications — as a means to catch up kids who are being lost in crowded, test-reliant, merit-funded schools. Of course, even Yang points out that schools are only one part of the puzzle. There’s screens and social media taking over our emotional lives and psychiatric development; the pandemic’s long-felt chilling effect on socialization; the adult world of division and anger in politics and everywhere else; and of course changes within the Mental Health Industrial Complex.

It’s this last piece that Dr. Sami Timimi, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychotherapist at the National Health Service in the United Kingdom is focused on. He's the author of six books including Naughty Boys: Anti-Social Behavior, ADHD, and the Role of Culture and his most recent book, Searching for Normal, which promises to outline a new approach to understanding mental health, distress and neurodiversity. There little doubt we could use some advice here — and a bit of demystification around the mental health crises that seems to have taken over childhood.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I frankly found Searching for Normal to be a difficult book. The science and ideas are very clearly laid out, but you're throwing a lot of stones systemically and culturally that are not often cast. As a layperson and a parent with a house filled with diagnoses, medications, cultural shame, and lots of doubts about our mental health journey, the paralysis you describe feels very close to home. Given all this, I'm wondering, big picture, what is the main takeaway you'd want a parent to walk away with from your book?

Dr. Sami Timimi: It is a difficult read because we have a public narrative that's been around for a while that's really created a mythology around what we think of in terms of mental health and behavioral difference. My main message is that what we are calling psychiatric diagnosis aren't really diagnoses. And be careful where the culture of diagnoses might lead you to, because we have so much evidence now that the way we're approaching mental health has resulted in something called the treatment prevention paradox, where at a population level we're seeing increasing prevalence of mental conditions and mental health diagnoses. At the same time we're seeing an increasing number of people accessing various types of treatments associated with these diagnoses.

But we're not seeing an improvement in the outcomes. If we saw an improvement in the outcomes, we would expect at least a stabilization and hopefully a reduction in prevalence of certain conditions because they would be being effectively treated. I don't think there's actually much disagreement with this in most of the academic literature on what's going on because mental health does seem to be an outlier compared to we've seen a lot of progress in physical health.

For example, when I was a kid, if I got leukemia, my chances of survival into adulthood was around 20%. Now it's around 80%. So this is what happens when you have approaches that are built on technical knowledge that allows you to understand what's going on and make specific treatments for it. But it seems to be the case in mental health that we're going in the wrong direction. What are the assumptions that go missing when we approach mental health as if it's physical health? Because we have to remember, there's no brain scan for ADHD, there's no blood test for anxiety. You can't examine a thought under a microscope. And it becomes difficult to sit in that area of uncertainty and curiosity.

You talk about the TikTok contagion of health disorders and you cite the, I think it was 2023 research about Canadian teen girls presenting with a variety of self-described disorders that are all relatively rare. I'm wondering if you can describe the phenomenon and then I wonder, what does it change for parents on the ground? We have to take their thoughts seriously, no?

Yeah, that's a difficult one, isn't it? It's interesting because I heard about this research from a colleague and friend of mine who's a psychiatrist in Canada who shared this paper and it happened just at the point where I was seeing that in my clinical work as well, I was seeing young people who were brought by their parents, parents very worried, with presentations that are generally considered to be quite rare presentations. So, for example, I saw a number of kids who were coming and saying that they had these Tourette's symptoms but they had no history of it. It's like it suddenly emerged.

It is hard because first of all, I don't blame social media for causing these things because actually a lot of this is narratives that's been suggested and started out. The bigger phenomena are these influencers who say that they have ADHD or autism or anxiety and they publicize it online and they talk about things that are signs of potentially having these conditions. And we have to remember, growing up is tough. Try to remember what I was like as a 13, 14-year-old — it is a struggle. There's a lot of changes going on.

You're in a phase of your life where you're seeking meaning and you're seeking belonging and you're involved in those existential type of scenarios where you're trying to figure out where do I fit in? What's my life all about? And so what's been happening is because they watch a lot of these things online with a lot of the influencers just taking up concepts that have been given to them by certain branches of academic psychiatry. And so what social media is doing is a kind of a social contagion. It's turbocharging these ideas and spreading them out.

This goes alongside a trend that's been happening in parenting.

I think a lot of parents have lost their trust that they know what they're doing. I think a lot of parents have lost their confidence. They feel the need to go to see a professional to try and understand. And it's difficult when a lot of the professionals are also involved in what I call the Mental Health Industrial Complex. This is how they get paid, this is how they earn a living.

And so one of the things that I do encourage parents to do is don't be scared of your children. Don't be scared of their intense emotions and don't be scared of conflict. Conflict happens. What has I think happened as we've exported the knowledge base to professionals is we've also developed a curious form of something that some people refer to as cognitive parenting. I know the concept of helicopter parenting, cognitive parenting is a little bit different where you try to reason things through, where you treat your children as if they're already developed adults.

If you don't think this is good for your children, tell them. If you want to put some boundaries around them, don't be afraid of their conflicts.

I liken it a little bit to a referee in, well, for us it's a soccer match. Whenever they, say, blow the whistle that there's a foul committed, the offending team that you've blown the whistle for will complain. That's what happens.

The crowd will complain as well and say the referee is biased and so on. So when you are a rule enforcer, one way to think about it is you're not going to get any good feedback. You're always going to get protests. You have to ride that out. But a good referee delivers the consequence. The consequence is usually fairly short, it's fairly immediate. Don't delay the consequences because you don't say, well, I've seen you doing that foul, but the next match you have, if you do that again, then the next match you have, I'm going to give this or that. Whatever consequence it is, immediate, short-lived, doesn't have to be long. Just something that shows that you disapprove and this is not allowed.

And the other thing you do is you don't argue with them. So in soccer matches, you have a half-time where the teams go into the dressing room for 15 minutes before coming. You don't see a referee running after the player who's committed the foul telling them, “I've seen you, I've seen you doing this in other matches. You think you're going to get away with it. You never learn, you never listen.” A good referee spots the infringement, knows that they're going to get back chatted and they're going to get flak, needs to develop a thick skin to ride that out, not rise to it and doesn't get involved in nagging them and so on. And once the consequence is delivered, it's over. Don't need to talk about it again. It's finished.

What happens when you get caught in what you call the Mental Health Industrial Complex? A quote in the book that really resonated with me, asks “What might happen if instead of shaping the treatment around diagnosis, it was put to one side and the specific challenges, fears, and context were engaged with instead?” Can you answer the question you pose? What does that exactly look like?

So one of the things, understanding that what we call psychiatric diagnoses are not actually diagnoses, they're descriptions. They're what a branch of therapy referred to as narrative therapy ...[which] basically says that our life is made up of stories. It's the stories we hear about ourselves, the stories others tell about us, and we build up a set of stories to understand ourselves. We're surrounded by narratives. And the narratives we tell ourselves have a powerful impact on how we experience our emotions.

So what I was describing there is instead of falling down the root of imagining that if you get a diagnosis you found the meaning for what it is that is going on that's troubling you, there is a different way of trying to find out what it is you're trying to achieve, what is it the difference that you're trying to make, that a diagnosis can't do. So one thing I do in my clinical life is a form of what's referred to as Socratic questioning.

Let's say you got a diagnosis and it was the perfect diagnosis and you felt it fitted. What difference do you imagine this is going to make to your life? What difference is that going to make to your life?

A diagnosis in a sense is an abstract thing. It doesn't really tell you specifically materially what's going on in your world. Is it that actually you're having trouble with friendships? Is it that your family is under stress and you're under stress because you think your parents are about to split up? Is it that you're finding yourself out of your depth at school? So you're trying to get to the specifics of what it is that people are wanting to see change in their life.

Right. Keep questioning the outcomes and ideas. I really like this tool for parents.

And the other thing is I'm trying to help people move past the idea that experiencing intense emotions is a sign that there's something wrong in them. Experiencing intense emotions is something that we all have to go through. If we don't go through it, we have less of a chance to develop psychologically.

In a sense, the role of parents is to be careful about saving your children from struggle and suffering because that is an unrealistic goal. All life involves struggle and suffering at some level. How can we know joy if we don't know sadness? It's impossible.

You say this is the most pathologized generation ever. Given that, do you have a checklist for parents to look through and say, is my child being pathologized?

That's an interesting question. I may be averse to the whole concept of checklists, partly because in understanding that all our definitions of mental health are subjective. So our understanding of what is and isn't a kind of looming problem that needs some sort of professional intervention. There is no formula that will allow you to figure this one out. It's going to have to be situation, person and family specific.

One thing I say to parents is, look, all good parents feel guilty. That's just a given. I cannot help you with that. Whatever I do, whatever anybody does, you'll carry on feeling guilty or worry, have I done too much of this? Have I interviewed too little? Have I given too much advice? Have I given the wrong? That's what good parents do. Be careful about that guilt driving you to do too much. And I think that's now a bigger danger than the opposite. So we end up intervening perhaps unnecessarily without holding our own anxiety and our own guilt. So one of my little messages is don't try too hard.

On that note, what do you do with the big feelings in a household? How do you let issues not get carried away?

So one of the things that I try to work with with families is understanding, I use the metaphor of a dance, that there's emotional flow going between people and that emotional flow defines how that relationship works. And sometimes what happens is that anger becomes the dominant way in which connection happens.

The other thing I think about in terms of emotions, I think of emotions as being viral. You catch the emotions of the person closest to you. If your kid is angry with you, it's very hard not to get angry back at them. So kind of developing an awareness of that emotional flow of how it's working in your particular relationship and developing an understanding that that has become a dance.

For example, I know there was a period in my own kid's life where there was a lot of tension, a lot of sibling rivalry to the point where our son and daughter were getting physical and losing temper. And we thought, me and my wife thought only one of them would survive in childhood. That's what it felt like to us.

Anyway, so I thought, okay, well I have to try and do something about this. So I started writing little post-its at the end of each day, just a few, a sentence or two about things that I liked that happened and I just stuck it above their bed before they went to bed.

After a couple of weeks of doing this, my daughter said to me, "Dad, you're being weird." And I said, "What do you mean I'm being weird?"

"Why do you keep putting these post-its and saying these nice things?" I said, "Okay, do you like it?"

So just something also a bit playful a bit, but it's just about trying to refine that emotional connection somewhere other than what's become the defining dance.

A little bit of, “all you need is love.” And I think you had it at the top of one of your chapters, quoting Confucius.

Exactly. The journey of a thousand miles starts with the first step.

#8110. These Were The Most Popular Baby Names Of 2026, According To BabyCenter

And what trends we may see more of in 2027.

Each year, BabyCenter compiles all the data from their users and publishes a list of the year’s most popular baby names. The official rankings from the Social Security Administration, based on actual issued birth certificates, usually don’t come in until months into the new year, so this is our first peek at which names might have been given to the most babies born in 2026. But they also spot names that have risen quickly in popularity, helping identify what’s coming next in baby-naming trends.

The most popular baby names of 2026 are a predictable pair: Olivia for girls and Noah for boys. Olivia was also the most popular girl name of 2025, according to the SSA, and Noah was #2 on the boys’ chart.

Here’s how the rest of the top 10 shook out, according to BabyCenter’s data:

Many of these names have fallen somewhere in the top 10 for multiple years running, but Evelyn in particular rejoins the chart after falling off in 2024. And five completely new monikers broke into the top 100 this year. Making their debuts are Magnolia, Milo, Dean, Archer, and Stetson.

Speaking of Magnolia, long baby names are generally gaining in popularity, according to BabyCenter’s report. In fact, 29% of the top girl names and 31% of the top boy names had seven or more letters (21% had four or less, by comparison). Perhaps parents are opting for longer names that sound good on an adult’s resume, with cute nickname options to use ‘til then.

If you’re big into initials, you’ll like to know that E is currently the most popular first initial for girls (15% of BabyCenter’s top 100 girl names begin with it), while J ranks highest for boys at 14%.

Western-inspired baby names have been trending for a couple of years now, and that doesn’t seem to be slowing down. BabyCenter noted big jumps in popularity for Stetson, Wilder, Callahan, Sadie, and Sutton, to name a few. Names that include an X got a lot of use this year too, according to BabyCenter’s Steph Coffield. Prepare to see even more baby Jaxsons, Maximillians, Ximenas, Xaidens, X-cetera (sorry).

And thanks of course to the eponymous movie, the name Odysseus rose an astronomical 1,456 spots on BabyCenter’s popularity charts. While it won’t be everyone’s first choice for a baby boy in the new year, it does seem like more parents are leaning into Greek mythology for name inspo. Monikers like Atlas, Ares, Evander, Daphne, and Gaia are all scooching their way up the rankings as we speak.

While it’s hard to say exactly what 2027’s baby name trends will bring (you never know when a pop culture moment like Odysseus will change the charts), we can’t wait to hear more interesting names being called across the playground.

#8109. Nobody told me I’d be too busy making the memories to enjoy them

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

By Jessica Koosed Etting Updated Oct. 21, 2026

A few weeks before my son Oliver turned eight, planning his birthday started taking up residence in my brain.

We weren’t aiming for anything particularly extravagant. We were having extended family over for dinner and cake, and enjoying the same traditions we’d built around birthdays over the years. Breakfast in bed with balloons. Presents. Time with grandparents. His favorite meal for dinner. And at the end of the night, we’d go around the table and each say three things we loved about him.

These little rituals have become the essence of our family’s birthday magic.

In the weeks leading up to the big day, I was thinking about what Oliver wanted, figuring out the food, doing the shopping, wrapping the gifts, finding cute decorations, coordinating with family about wish lists, ordering the cake, making sure his brothers had something to give him, and remembering the special cereal he wanted. I was doing all of that alongside work and school and dinner and everything else our family already had going on.

Then the birthday came, and it all went off as planned, for the most part. Oliver was thrilled. His brothers were excited. Our family was there. At one point, the boys were all playing and laughing together with their grandparents, and I remember wanting to go sit with them.

Instead, my brain took over. If I didn’t start clearing dinner now, we’d get the cake too late, and we still needed to have time for presents.

So I got up. Set up the cake and dessert. Found the candles I’d bought. Rounded everyone up. Took pictures. And then came more dishes and wrapping paper to clean up and wrangling three tired kids into bed.

Later that night, I sat down and looked through the photos on my phone of everyone smiling together. They were exactly the kind of pictures that make you think, This. This is the good stuff.

But, I couldn’t remember a single moment where I had really enjoyed it or even felt present with my son the whole night. And, unfortunately, birthdays weren’t the only time I felt like this.

I always thought I’d be the type of mom who loved creating fun memories for my kids. Until I became a parent, I never realized how much invisible labor it took to create those magical moments of childhood.

Tooth fairy rituals, holiday traditions, family vacations and weekend outings… They all require someone planning things out in advance. And, usually, that someone is Mom.

To be clear, I love creating fun moments for our family. I know it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it wasn’t something I personally wanted to give up. But something needed to change.

Because, while I was busy planning and managing the entire experience, I wasn’t participating. Instead of enjoying my time on the beach with the kids, I was already thinking about who needed sunscreen re-application, or the groceries we’d need to grab for the next day, or the email I needed to send back to their coach.

Some of that is unavoidable. But all of it didn’t have to be mine.

I wish I could say I simply decided to be more present, but it took years to build better habits around how our family plans and shares the work, and I still catch myself slipping into cruise-director mode sometimes.

But as the founder of Jam, an all-in-one calendar and organization app to reduce the mental load of modern family life, I’ve also spent a lot of time thinking about how to better manage the invisible labor that piles up. And over the years, I’ve found some tried-and-true ways to alleviate it, especially during those special magical moments.

Over time, I also realized that some of the most special moments with my kids require absolutely no planning at all. A slow Sunday morning when nobody has anywhere to be. A few extra cuddles and arm tickles at bedtime. The last ice cream cone of summer, before “real life” starts again.

But those moments are also so easy to miss when half your brain is already in tomorrow.

Now I’m better at recognizing that constant pull of the mental load, and pressing pause on it, too.

There will always be something that needs to happen next. I’m a working mom with three kids, after all, so it’s unavoidable.  But I am more aware now that I don’t want to spend their childhood constantly preparing for the next part of it. Sometimes Sunday morning is a good time to get a jump on a few things that need to get done… and sometimes, it isn’t.

When I look back at the pictures, I want to see more than the beautiful moments I created for my kids.

I want to remember how it felt to be there with them, too.
