#8031. Chatting About Weird Cat Behaviors, Hissing, & Cats Who Hump | Chatty Cattys, Episode 37

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

In this episode of Catster's Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole dive deep into the peculiar yet normal world of feline behavior, unraveling the mysterious reasons behind common cat habits. From unpacking why domestic pets bring home "gifts" like dead prey or hair ties to setting the record straight on why cats "make biscuits," they share what it truly means to listen to, understand, and care for our feline companions. Instead of advertising a one-size-fits-all approach to pet discipline, the conversation focuses on the importance of understanding a cat's instincts and body language. The hosts chat about how speaking a cat's natural language leads to better communication, proving that forcing a feline into a human mold rarely ends well.

Tune in to find out why your indoor or outdoor cat feels driven to bring home dead preyâor stolen household objects like hair tiesâeven when they are fully fed. Dr. Karyn breaks down the hardwired hunting instincts that persist despite domestication, explaining how cats view their owners as substitute family members to provide for. You will also learn about the true origin of kneading (or "making biscuits"), why it brings adult cats so much comfort, and why some male cats awkwardly take the habit a step further.

Plus, this episode sheds light on hilarious personal pet stories. You will find out what happened when Dr. Karyn caught her neutered cat making eyes at her while humping a cozy blanket, why traditional deterrents like spray bottles or double-sided tape often backfire into fun games, and how a simple, gentle "hiss" can instantly communicate boundaries to your pet!

Hunting Instincts Realities: Dr. Karyn and Nicole address why cats bring home dead animals or scavenged items, clarifying that hunting is an automatic survival drive with no time for logical processing, meaning even well-fed cats will pounce on instinct.

Klepto Cats & Treasure Hunting: The hosts reveal that some cats redirect their hunting drive entirely onto non-living household items, such as hair ties, bringing "treasure" home to their owners as part of their natural drive to provide for their substitute family.

The "Making Biscuits" Origin: Dr. Karyn explains that kneading originates from suckling behaviors in kittenhood; while grown cats no longer need to nurse, they carry the motion into adulthood because it triggers a cozy, endorphin-filled state of comfort and security.

Arousal and Humping Habits: The episode explores how kneading can sometimes lead to unexpected sexual arousal or humping in cats, noting that while humping is typically associated with dog dominance, cats display it purely as a cozy or quirky behavior rather than a social hierarchy tool.

Misinterpreting Body Language: Dr. Karyn clarifies that cat facial expressions and body language require full context; wide pupils can mean fight-or-flight adrenaline or catnip excitement, while a swishing tail can signal playfulness or an impending scratch.

Effective Boundaries Over Punishment: The hosts highlight why yelling, spray bottles, or double-sided tape fail to stop bad behavior, sharing Dr. Karyn's top tip of using a brief, clear "hiss" to instantly speak their language and set boundaries without causing distress.

#8030. 10 Foreign True Crime Documentaries To Scratch Two Itches At Once

Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? Why not do both?

Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? It’s the universal conundrum. On the one hand, the world is a big and beautiful place full of opportunities to eat delicious food and meet new people and wear hats you would never wear at home. On the other hand, there are true crime stories that need to be solved by you in your pajamas on the couch under a weighted blanket.

How do you scratch both of those itches? Well, you could travel the world seeking out true crimes to solve yourself, but that would get pricey and probably pretty dangerous. You don’t want to become the subject of your own true crime documentary, after all. Instead, settle in on a long, rainy weekend (or when it’s bright and sunny, I’m not judging) to watch these engrossing true crime documentaries set in beautiful locations around the world. It’s safer and the snacks are cheaper.

In 1996, French film producer Sophie Toscan du Plantier was found murdered outside her remote holiday cottage in the small village of Toormore. West Cork two days before Christmas. Sophie was just 39 years old and mom to son Pierre-Louis. A local journalist was one of the first to report her murder, and quickly became the main suspect. Netflix’s three-part docuseries Sophie - A Murder in West Cork covers not only Sophie’s tragic death, but also the struggle between Ireland and France to convict the killer.

Amy Lynn Bradley was just 23 years old when she went missing from the Royal Caribbean cruise ship Rhapsody of the Sea one early morning in March 1998. The ship was en route to the island of Curaçao. Her room showed no sign of a struggle, and several items were left behind. Authorities initially considered Bradley’s disappearance to be a potential accident or suicide, but Netflix’s 2025 three-part docuseries Amy Bradley is Missing speculates on several other possibilities that could have happened in the sunny tropics.

We do not love a scam artist. Especially one who preys on women looking for love, as Israeli conman Shimon Hayut aka Simon Leviev did between 2017 to 2019. Hayut swindled millions of dollars from women in the Netherlands, Norway, and other countries around Europe, leaving them destitute and broken-hearted. That’s the bad news. The good news is the way these women eventually found each other, banding together to bring Hayut to justice and try to reclaim their money. Netflix’s 2022 documentary The Tinder Swindler tells the story of three women who lost nearly everything to Hayut, and how they came together to bring him down.

The Netflix 2026 three-part docuseries Should I Marry a Murderer? will stay with you for a long time after the fact. Not just because it’s set in the gorgeous Scottish countryside, but because of the perspective it offers on what it might actually look like to find out the man you love is genuinely a murderer. Caroline Muirhead met handsome Scottish farmer Alexander “Sandy” McKellar on Tinder, and the two got engaged in 2020 after a whirlwind four month romance. When McKellar confessed to a murder that happened three years earlier, Muirhead stays with him. Told from her modern day perspective, Should I Marry a Murderer? Is an unflinching glimpse at what we might be willing to overlook in the name of love.

Vittorio Emanuele was nine years old when his family was exiled from Italy in 1946. His father was King Umberto II, and Vittorio was meant to be a prince until Italy voted to create a republic without the royal family. Living a life of luxurious exile, Vittorio was on the French island of Corsica in 1978 when he was involved in the death of 19-year-old German tourist Dirk Hamer. Netflix’s 2023 three-part series The King Who Never Was features interviews with Vittorio himself, as well as Dirk Hamer’s family members who were determined to see the privileged deposed royal charged with Dirk’s murder.

Michel Fourniret confessed to killing 11 women and one man in the picturesque Ardennes region of France between 1987 to 2003, making him one of the most notorious serial killers in modern French history. The Belgian killer only confessed after his seemingly submissive wife, Monique Olivier, provided police with enough information to force his hand. Which meant, of course, that she knew something of her husband’s crimes. More than police might have suspected, if the 2023 Netflix limited series Monique Olivier: Accessory to Evil proves anything. Olivier might have even been a willing participant in her husband’s horrific crimes. Chilling.

Fair warning for the 2019 five-part Netflix docuseries Who Killed Little Gregory? - the entire series revolves around the awful kidnapping and murder of 4-year-old Grégory Villemin in a small village in eastern France. Grégory’s murder has never been solved, and this docuseries delves into the disturbing allegations that members of his own extended family might have murdered the little boy. This one is equal parts difficult to watch and completely engrossing.

If you’re looking for some real-life Scandinavian noir to get you through the dark nights of fall, you’ll want to check out The Lørenskog Disappearance, Netflix’s five-part docuseries based on the true story of real life Norwegian billionaire Tom Hagan. Hagan’s wife Anne-Elisabeth Hagan went missing from the couple’s opulent home in October 2018, and a ransom note asking for nine million euros was left in her wake. The police originally believed Anne-Elisabeth was kidnapped, but began to suspect murder when the alleged kidnappers didn’t continue to reach out. While this 2022 limited series is a drama and not a straight documentary, it really delivers on Scandi vibes and billionaire intrigue.

British tourist Grace Millane was taking a gap year to travel the world when she ended up in New Zealand in 2018. She planned to head back home to her family for Christmas. She never made it back home. Millane was reported missing by her family, with police conducting a massive search in Auckland and the surrounding area before zeroing in on Jesse Kempson, her final Tinder date. The 2024 documentary The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane on Amazon Prime, features interview tapes with Kempson as he is interrogated by police, and his subsequent attempt to use the so-called “rough sex murder” defense for killing the 22-year-old. On her birthday.

If you’ve been thinking of spending a bit of time in the UK along the coast, the Apple TV series Coastal Killers will either intrigue you or scare you off, depending on your perspective. #8028. Self-Gifting Ideas For Moms: 28 Holiday Gifts To Treat Yourself

Oh, we’re stuffing our own stockings again? Well, they’re gonna be filled with things we love, gosh damn it.

Every December, moms pull off a small miracle, and we do it mostly on our own. The presents get bought, wrapped, and tucked under the tree with tender care. The stockings get stuffed, the Elf gets Shelf’ed, the fridge and pantry get filled with foods everyone in the family (even your little picky eater) will enjoy. And nearly every December, moms end up with an empty stocking or whatever drugstore special got picked up last-minute because, oops, Mom doesn’t have anything under the tree again!

If your family actually remembers to toss a present or two under the tree or in the stocking for you, you’ve probably grown accustomed to getting the same gift, or some variation of it, every year. A “World’s Best Mom” mug. A bath bomb. You know the type. It’s fine. Really. We know it’s the thought that counts! But we also know that moms spend the entire holiday season thinking about everyone else’s wish lists, and nobody’s thinking very hard about ours.

That’s exactly why we here at Scary Mommy are big fans of taking matters into our own hands. Buy these gifts for yourself, stuff your own stocking, use ‘em to drop some very unsubtle hints on your partner’s phone, or forward this list straight to your friends and family. Because you, dear friend, deserve gifts you’ll genuinely love... and not another GD bath bomb (unless that’s your thing).

Every time I put these on the bed, my husband and I waller around like piggies in mud. They're so soft! You must waller, smiling with your eyes shut, to really enjoy them. I adore everything about these sheets and am jonesing to replace some of our old cheap sheet sets with more. They feel breathable, don't make my night sweats worse like cheap sheets do, and they actually STAY on our mattress. We all know there's nothing worse than laying on a bunch of wrinkles all night once your fitted sheet pops off a corner. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

For the woman on your holiday list who is thoughtful about what goes on her skin, this is such a beautiful and meaningful gift. The Golden Beryl Moisturizer is a lightweight, non-greasy daily hydrator packed with organic turmeric root, ginger root, bearberry extract, hyaluronic acid, CoQ10, and Vitamin C, all formulated to brighten, even tone, and support the skin barrier without a harsh ingredient in sight. The entire Golden Beryl Collection is hormone-conscious, Leaping Bunny certified, pregnancy-safe, and free from parabens, phthalates, sulfates, and synthetic fragrances, which in clean beauty is genuinely rare. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

Ever since having my delightful children 10+ years ago, I've been on — shall we say — a hair journey. My hair has done the postpartum fall out, it's done the regrowth, and now, years later, it's graying, changing texture, and, once again, falling out. This stuff is great to help combat that, plus it makes my hair super shiny. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief

If you've been waiting for someone to get you a red light therapy mask, and they just haven't, well, now is your time, girl! I love this one because it's so comfortable and looks so lovely — while delivering 360-degree red light coverage that's FDA-approved. I'm all about beauty finds that are evidence-based, and this fits the ticket. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

Everyone who has ever set foot in my house knows I almost always have at least one candle burning. I just think it makes everything feel so cozy and welcoming! And this candle subscription box is the perfect thing to keep me stocked and happy. With the Luxe Box, you get two 16-ounce soy candles every month from different independent American candle makers. I really appreciate the little backstories included, and how they highlight women- and minority-owned makers. The candles smell DIVINE, and they come in super frickin’ cute little printed cloth bags. It’s just such a fun treat to look forward to each month. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

I have been eyeing this Noon & Moon mug for literal years. It's so pretty and cozy and cottagecore, but the price point always had me closing out of the tab without adding to cart. But isn't that the kind of item, the one you usually won't buy yourself but know you'll use and love so often, that makes the perfect gift? — Katie McPherson

This palette is on my personal wish list, and I cannot stop thinking about it. Chokehold Cosmetics is an indie brand, and this palette delivers on that with seven highly pigmented eyeshadow shades, from soft matte beige to molten gold shimmer to blood red, plus a warm blush and an unapologetic highlighter, all in one gorgeous compact. It is vegan, cruelty-free, and the shade names alone — Undressed, Shackle, Bite Mark, Blood Oath — tell you exactly the kind of energy this brand is bringing. — Katie Garrity

I have tried every single water bottle and tumbler cup on the market, and I mean every.single.one. This one is my favorite. It sips like a straw (but the shape means no mouth wrinkles!), doesn't hurt my sensitive teeth, the straw never falls out and forces me to stick my hands into the water to get it so I can keep drinking...and yes, it keeps my water cold forever. I was worried the snap-shut lid wouldn't be strong enough to stay closed, and maybe if you want to toss your water bottle in a bag and not worry about it at all, it wouldn't. But for someone who carries their water bottle and at most lays it down in the seat of my car, it has prevented spills just fine. And bless, it doesn't spurt water up at you when it's been closed and jostled around a little. That's my pet peeve. — Katie McPherson

Harry & David’s Moose Munch is the iconic caramel popcorn drizzled with chocolate and loaded with premium mix-ins that has been a cult holiday snack for decades, and for very good reason. It is the kind of treat that sits on the counter and disappears faster than you planned for, and the holiday tins and gift boxes make it feel genuinely special rather than just a bag of snacks. It’s the “buy it for yourself” gift that you absolutely deserve and will not regret for a single second! — Katie Garrity

I burn candles constantly, and I love finding a new candle brand to try out. Paddywax makes some of the cutest candle vessels that you'll want to keep long after the wax runs out. The teak wood is smooth, sturdy, scratch-free on nonstick cookware, and has a warm, beautiful grain that makes the whole kitchen feel pulled together just by sitting out. — Katie Garrity

I'd never smelled a Fulton & Roark fragrance until this year, and now I'm obsessed with multiple. Calle Ocho is a gourmand lover's dream. Lover's Lane has a gorgeous deep fruity vibe that I keep reaching for in winter, while Hwy 190 was my summer go-to. The Discovery sets are a great way to smell a range of options from the brand, and they come with a $30 coupon code to spend on a full-size perfume once you pick your favorite. In short, they scream "stuff me in a stocking." — Katie McPherson

This set has completely elevated my morning skincare routine, and it is the buy-it-for-yourself gift that actually gets used every single day. The Sweet July Morning Essentials Set includes the Pava Exfoliating Cleanser, Pava Toner, Soursop Vitamin C Serum, and Castaway Cream, all inspired by founder Ayesha Curry’s Jamaican heritage and packed with Caribbean superfoods like papaya, guava, and soursop that make your skin look genuinely luminous. Everything is clean, vegan, cruelty-free, and formulated for all skin tones and types, which means it actually works rather than just sitting on a shelf looking pretty. It’s the morning routine upgrade that makes getting out of bed worth it because your skin is going to look that good. — Katie Garrity

You want to pick out your own skincare anyway, but if you send this to your partner on a wishlist you'll probably have to hear about the price. But if you have extremely dry skin that has never responded well to retinol of any kind, I beg you to put this under the tree for yourself. My skin will not tolerate retinol at all, but this product gives me the healthiest plump and glow without any irritation. I've had numerous people ask me what I'm doing differently with my skin since I started using it (and because it's gentle enough to use multiple nights a week, I actually get results, not just flakes and irritation). — Katie McPherson

This is genuinely one of my favorite discoveries of the year and absolutely qualifies as a gift to yourself. Delta makes hemp-derived THC sparkling beverages in the most delicious flavors that deliver a light, relaxing buzz without the next-morning regret that comes with alcohol. Each can has a precise, low dose so you always know exactly what you are getting; the effect is that perfect mellow, calm feeling that makes a Tuesday night on the couch feel like a genuine treat, and they taste like something a fancy cocktail bar would charge way too much for. — Katie Garrity

Jasmine Dowling Plum Polka Dot Phone Case

Look, I get not wanting to spend a ton of money on a phone case, but recently I realized how much I use them and how much better a good one protects my very expensive little pocket computer. The Dairy's are so pretty and on trend, and I love all the matching accessories. They're tough too. I snagged a MagSafe case so I can use a magnetic grip on the back (helps my wrists), as well as the matching battery pack for when I'm out and about and suddenly realize I'm at 10%. Also, I love that they commission designs from real artists for their cases (this one is by Jasmine Dowling). — Katie McPherson

These notecards are one of those purchases that make you feel like a more elevated version of yourself. The Liberty London floral prints are absolutely stunning, the paper quality is thick and luxurious, and there is something genuinely joyful about having a set of notecards this beautiful sitting on your desk ready to go. Sending a handwritten note feels like a lost art, and this set makes you want to bring it back immediately, whether it is a thank you, a thinking of you, or just an excuse to use something this pretty. — Katie Garrity

I’ve been wanting to try Prose custom hair and skincare for so long; the holidays feel like the perfect time to treat myself! I am loving using shampoo, conditioner, and skincare formulated specifically for my needs, goals, and routine. You just take their quick (but thorough) online consultation and, voila, Prose whips up stuff just for you. They even put your name on the bottles! I think this would make such a thoughtful gift for another mom, or even for a teen. We got my 15-year-old a set, and they’re just as hooked as I am. — Julie Sprankles

This sweatshirt is the buy-it-for-yourself purchase that requires absolutely zero justification. It is cozy, it is Winnie the Pooh, and it makes every single person who sees you wearing it immediately smile, which is honestly a public service. The fit is relaxed and comfortable without being shapeless, the graphic is that perfect nostalgic Disney art style that hits every millennial who grew up watching the Hundred Acre Wood, and it is the kind of piece you reach for on every cozy fall and winter morning without thinking twice. Permission granted to add to cart immediately! — Katie Garrity

For the woman who takes her candles seriously, this is the one worth buying for yourself this season. The Amélie is a warm, complex, deeply luxurious blend of saffron and oud that fills a room without being overwhelming, and it has that rich, sophisticated scent profile that makes your home smell like a boutique hotel rather than a Yankee Candle. La Jolie Muse uses natural soy wax, cotton wicks, and fragrance oils that actually throw scent properly rather than disappearing after twenty minutes. — Katie Garrity

Over the years, my makeup routine has become much more streamlined. I don’t have time for a 12-step routine, but I do have time for two steps that make me look and feel way more put-together than I actually am most days. And this Iconic Londo duo happens to come with both of those products, which, for the record, are consistent refills for me. The Underglow Blurring Primer is hands-down my go-to primer; it smooths over my pores, makes my makeup glide on beautifully, and gives me that dreamy soft-focus finish. Then I finish with the cult-favorite Prep-Set-Glow mist, which leaves my skin dewy and radiant. — Julie Sprankles

I love having high-quality, soft-as-heck blankets all over my house. I think it's one of the main things that makes people tell me how cozy my home is. These glasses are one of my favorite things I own, and they make every drink feel like an occasion. Bogg bags have been having a serious moment for a while now, and the Go Tote is the version that makes the most sense for everyday life. Menifee, California â September 28, 2026 â Petra Luna, creator of the CatCrazy Channel and founder of CatCrazy, has received four Certificates of Excellence (COE) in the 2026 Cat Writersâ Association (CWA) Communications Contest in the Video, Film, or Television Production category.

The recognition adds to the three Certificates of Excellence Luna received in the 2025 CWA Communications Contest, bringing her total to seven CWA Certificates of Excellence over the past two years.

For Luna, the awards represent more than recognition for individual videos. They reflect the mission that has driven CatCrazy since she launched the channel in 2019: helping cat parents better understand their cats and make more informed decisions about their care, nutrition, and the products they bring into their homes.

Luna's journey into cat education began after the loss of two beloved cats, Chopin and Wazoo, following what she describes as a devastating experience involving treats she had trusted.

The experience changed the way she looked at the products she was giving her cats â and ultimately changed the direction of her life and career.

She didn't set out to become a cat-food entrepreneur. She became one because of what happened to her cats.

âI started creating content because I wanted cat parents to have better information and to ask questions about the things we often take for granted,â says Luna. âThere is so much information out there, and sometimes it can be difficult to know what to believe. I wanted to help cat parents become better informed and more confident advocates for their cats.â

Luna's work as a cat educator eventually led her to an unexpected next step: creating her own cat food.

Today, CatCrazy offers Puckinâ Crazy Chicken Feast, a premium freeze-dried raw cat food created specifically for cats. The food is made in the USA and formulated to be complete and balanced for cats of all life stages.

âCreating our own cat food was a natural extension of that mission,â Luna says. âIf I'm going to talk about what cats deserve, I also want to create something I genuinely believe is worthy of feeding to my own cats.â

CatCrazy's approach combines education with a consumer product, giving Luna an opportunity to address both sides of the equation: helping cat parents understand what they are feeding their cats while creating a food she feels good about feeding her own.

The 2026 CWA Communications Contest recognizes outstanding cat-focused work across a wide range of media. This year's entries came from Australia, Belgium, Canada, Egypt, Great Britain, New Zealand, Japan, Puerto Rico and 28 U.S. states.

Contest categories include publications, articles published in print or online, poetry and fiction, non-fiction books, digital and broadcast media, and images. CatCrazy is a cat-focused media and pet food company founded by Petra Luna. Beginning with the CatCrazy Channel in 2019, the company has grown into a community dedicated to helping cat parents better understand, care for, and advocate for their cats.

CatCrazy's first food product, Puckinâ Crazy Chicken Feast, is a premium freeze-dried raw cat food formulated to be complete and balanced for cats of all life stages. The organization was created to help provide good information about cats to the general public and support writers dedicated to that effort.

Today, the CWA has approximately 300 members representing a wide variety of talents and media, including journalism, social media, graphic design, writing, radio, television, videography, podcasts, websites, blogs, photography, illustration, cartoons and more.

#8026. Broadway Stars Shine and Shelter Dogs Take Center Stage at the Fetch Pet Gala!

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

When a room fills with Broadway stars, an evening at The Carlyle could easily become another glamorous New York event. But on October 19, the spotlight wonât be on those performing onstage; it will be shining on shelter dogs looking for homes.

The second annual Fetch Pet Gala will bring musical superstars Bernadette Peters, Darren Criss, and Ariana DeBose together for a night of performances, dinner, and fundraising in support of pets and the people who care for them. Hosted by Fetch Pet Insurance, the gala has already sold out, with an overflowing waitlist.

The evening will begin with a Green Carpet featuring adoptable dogs from North Shore Animal League America, one of the countryâs largest no-kill animal rescue and adoption organizations. The dogs will have a chance to bathe in the limelight and meet potential adopters before guests head into CafÃ© Carlyle for dinner and performances.

For anyone who works with animals, the purpose behind a night like this is easy to recognize. Giving a pet a second chance often takes much more than finding an empty spot on someone's couch. There may be veterinary care, foster placement, rehabilitation, transportation, or other support needed before a dog or cat is ready to start over.

Sometimes, getting an animal ready for adoption means more than just a makeover. Addressing problems that have been overlooked for months or even years, like dental disease, skin conditions, parasites, chronic pain, and behavioral challenges can all become part of the journey toward a new home.

The same is true for pets already living with families. When people face illness or financial hardship, keeping up with a pet's needs can become difficult, even when the bond between them remains as strong as ever.

For many pet parents, the idea of giving up a beloved animal is heartbreaking. But when money is tight or a family is dealing with a serious illness, even routine veterinary care can suddenly feel out of reach.

That is where the Fetch Pet Gala becomes about much more than a glamorous night in New York. Behind the performances and the photographs are animals waiting for a second chance and families desperate to keep caring for the pets they love. The money raised can help transform lives in more ways than one.

For these dogs, walking the Green Carpet is much more than a glamorous photo opportunity. They are there in search of a happy ending to their story.

North Shore Animal League America works with animals rescued from overcrowded shelters, puppy mills, and natural disasters, preparing them for adoption by providing veterinary care and other support. Since its inception, more than 1.2 million animals have been saved through the organizationâs efforts.

Putting adoptable dogs in the middle of an evening filled with Broadway stars is a pretty effective way to remind us that rescue animals deserve their own spotlight, too. And maybe, just maybe, their Broadway moment will end with a happily ever after.

Once the Green Carpet wraps up, guests will move into CafÃ© Carlyle for dinner and performances from Peters, Criss, and DeBose.

Peters brings a particularly strong connection between Broadway and animal welfare. She co-founded Broadway Barks with Mary Tyler Moore, an organization that brings Broadway performers and animal shelters together to help dogs and cats find homes.

Criss and DeBose bring their own Broadway credentials to the evening. Criss, known by many for playing Blaine Anderson on televisionâs musical superhit, âGleeâ, recently earned a Tony Award for his performance in Maybe Happy Ending. Not to be outshone, DeBose won the 2022 Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Anita in Steven Spielbergâs remake of West Side Story.

The evening will conclude with the Fetch Pet After Party and another performance from a surprise guest. Last year it was John Legend, so the bar has been set pretty high for this yearâs mystery guest!

The celebrities and performances may be what catch people's attention, but the real purpose of the gala is fundraising.

The 2026 gala will benefit four organizations: Broadway Cares/Equity Fights AIDS, Broadway Barks, Wags & Walks, and North Shore Animal League America. Together, their work touches different parts of the challenges facing pets and the people who care for them, from shelter and adoption services to helping families continue caring for their animals during difficult circumstances.

Broadway Cares is supporting another side of the human-animal relationship. Through grants to organizations around the country, it helps people living with HIV/AIDS and other serious illnesses, including programs that help them continue caring for their pets. When someone is dealing with a serious illness or financial hardship, paying for a pet's food, medications, or veterinary visits can become difficult. For veterinary professionals, this is a familiar reality: the ability to pay for care can sometimes determine what happens next for an animal, even when the family desperately wants to do what is best for them. Yet giving up a beloved animal can be another painful loss at an already difficult time. Helping people meet their pets' basic needs can allow those animals to stay where they belong: with the people who love them.

Wags & Walks focuses on rescue dogs and reducing euthanasia, while Broadway Barks works to connect shelter animals with adoptive families. North Shore Animal League America brings the rescue and adoption side directly into the gala through the dogs appearing on the Green Carpet.

The Fetch Pet Gala is still a relatively new event, but its first year showed what this combination of entertainment and philanthropy can accomplish.

The Fetch Pet Gala is part of a greater charitable effort from Fetch Pet Insurance. The company says it has raised more than $14.6 million for organizations and initiatives supporting pets, animals, and the people who care for them.

For the 2026 event, the formula remains much the same: bring people together, put rescue animals in the spotlight, and turn an evening of entertainment into funding for organizations doing hands-on work. And ultimately, that is what makes a night like this worth paying attention to.

The dresses, performances, and famous faces will make for a wonderful night, but the heart of the evening is in the animals waiting for a family and in the people doing everything they can to keep their pets healthy and by their side. After all, a pet's home is more than a place to live. It is where they are loved, cared for, and, very often, where they are part of the family.

The Green Carpet may be where the night begins, but for the dogs waiting for homes and the families trying to care for their pets through difficult circumstances, the impact of the evening will extend well beyond one fun night in New York.

Think your vegetable garden is finished for the year? Not so fast. Some crops relish cooler temperatures and can shrug off a little frost.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November doesn’t necessarily mark the end of the vegetable growing season. While warm-season crops are definitely done for the year, you may still be able to sow and grow some of your cold-hardy favorites.

Knowing how and when to plant a vegetable garden so late in the season depends on your USDA hardiness zone, climate, and local weather. If you have milder winters, you can likely sow seeds directly in outdoor beds. In colder climates, you’ll need to provide some protection against frost and snow.

Here, I offer pro tips on late veggie growing, along with eight vegetables you may be able to start now for a winter or spring harvest. If you’re unsure about whether or not you can grow any of these in November, contact your extension office for more location-specific guidance.

Planting veggies now takes more effort than simply sowing seeds. Beyond knowing your climate and hardiness zone, you need to pay attention to the weather. For example, avoid seeding when the soil is frozen or soggy.

Prepare the soil by clearing out weeds, raking out any stones or remaining summer plant debris, and mixing in fresh compost. Seed planting depth and spacing depend on the crop you are sowing, so do check the seed packet information.

Manage your expectations for this project. Less sunlight and colder temperatures mean germination and growth will be slow. Be patient.

Although these veggies are either cold-tolerant or good at overwintering, they still will not tolerate very cold weather. If you have cold winters, you’ll need to protect your efforts. An old milk jug can give seeds some protection and act as a mini greenhouse for a few seeds. If you want to start more seeds, use a cold frame, like the Giantex wooden cold frame, which has a flip top for easy access.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As plants develop, row covers will protect winter veggies from frost, snow, harsh winds, and flying pests. This Plant Covers Freeze Protection Kit on Amazon includes hoops, clips, and a roll of frost blanket.

Apply straw, shredded leaves, or other loose, organic mulch over and around new crops or overwintering veggies. Just take care not to drown delicate seedlings in mulch.

Take care with watering, as letting soil get soggy is easy to do in winter. Check the soil before watering plants.

These are some of our favorite vegetables that many gardeners can start in November, including those that could be ready in winter and others that you’ll harvest in spring or summer.

Garlic is an example of a crop that will overwinter and provide you with a harvest next summer. As long as your soil is workable and not waterlogged, garlic is a dependable crop for planting now. Plant individual garlic cloves with the pointy ends up. Use mulch to protect the cloves from winter freezes. If successful, your cloves will grow roots over winter, foliage in spring, and bulbs in the summer.

You can plant garlic from the grocery store, though it’s usually a softneck variety grown in milder climates and may struggle in colder regions. Hardneck garlic is often a better choice for those areas. Botanical Interests offers an organic garlic flavor sampler bundle featuring two hardneck varieties and elephant garlic.

Shallots can also be overwintered and will reward you with a harvest in late spring or early summer. Plant shallot sets or individual shallot bulbs with the pointy ends up, just slightly above the soil surface. French Red Shallots from Burpee are a delicious culinary variety worth trying.

You should mulch lightly to protect shallots in colder climates. However, fall planting is best suited to milder regions, and if you have very cold winters, the planting window may already have passed. Check with your local extension office for exact dates.

Spinach is remarkably cold-hardy. The seeds will be slow to germinate in the cold, though. This Sow Right Seeds Spinach Seed Collection contains three tasty varieties. Unless you have very mild winters, use cold frames or other protections. Once spinach plants get established, they should produce leaves you can pick throughout the winter. Harvest from the outside edge of the plants, leaving the center intact.

Kale is another very cold-hardy vegetable that many gardeners can grow now for winter harvests. It’s also hard to grow from seed in the cold, so unless you have mild weather in November, consider using transplants, like these Bonnie Plants Lacinato Kale Plants from Lowe's. Use cold frames or row covers as needed, especially during hard freezes. For warmer zones, Burpee sells a four-variety kale blend.

Arugula is a mildly cold-tolerant green that is best for growing in November in milder climates. If conditions are right, it will germinate and grow rapidly, giving you a winter harvest. If you want to grow arugula in colder regions, use frames or a greenhouse and be prepared for growth to be slower. You can pick up a pack of arugula seeds for less than $5 from Sow Right Seeds.

Like arugula, radishes grow rapidly, so if the weather and soil conditions are right, you can start plants now and get a quick winter harvest. Burpee's Cooks Custom Blend Radish Seeds Collection contains red, pink, purple, and white radishes. For the best results, the soil should be workable, and November temperatures should be cool or mild. For colder areas, plant the most cold-tolerant varieties and use cold frames.

Plant carrots now for a sweet treat in early spring. Carrots generally overwinter well, but choose the more cold-tolerant varieties for the best results. Scarlet Nantes, included in this Gardeners Basics 5-Variety Pack on Amazon, can be harvested through winter with protection. It’s also important to make sure the soil is loose and free of stones, so the roots can grow deep. Use a generous layer of mulch to keep the soil warmer over winter.

Peas can also generally be overwintered for a spring harvest. Peas grow best in cooler weather, but they still need some warmth to establish. Alaska peas, available from Eden Brothers, tolerate chilly conditions, but if your November is very cold, it might be too late. In milder growing regions, this can be a good time to start peas. Be sure to plant your peas near a trellis or other vertical structure so the plants can climb in spring.

November doesn’t have to mean the end of growing veggies for the year. Depending on your region and local weather, you may be able to grow or overwinter some or all of these cold-tolerant vegetables. Choose the plants most suited to your conditions and be patient. Colder weather means slower growth.

#8024. How To Initiate Sex Again After A Long Drought, Because We've All Been There

It’s all about easing in (and examining what got you here.)

Work, kids, family obligations, running your household, a hobby if you’re lucky enough to have time for one — all of these things take time and energy. It’s enough to have you laid out on the couch, carcass style, at the end of a regular day. When something actually goes wrong, like the kids get sick or a work project keeps you at your desk late, it’s even harder to imagine getting it up at the end of the day. No matter how much you love your spouse, sex droughts come for everyone at some point (ahem, many points) throughout a relationship. If it’s been a while and you want to get back in the game, here’s how to reinitiate.

Even when you’ve been married for years, once you and your partner get in a routine of not having sex, it can feel awkward or strange to try and start it up again. It almost feels like you have to acknowledge the drought, and therefore the bad things that led up to it, or perhaps the parts you’ve both played in letting it drag on. It’s just a lot, but try not to blame yourself.

“Sex droughts are far more common than pop culture would have us believe. They're certainly nothing to be ashamed of, nor do they represent a ‘failure,’” says Angie Rowntree, ABS, board-certified sexologist and founder and filmmaker behind the award-winning ethical adult film site Sssh.com. “Life happens. Bodies get sick or injured, or may have different needs. Children are born and demand your time and care. Older parents may need care. Jobs might change. Any number of stresses and interruptions in your life can upend what was your regularly scheduled Saturday date night or sap you of the carefree mojo you’d usually bring to the bedroom. None of that is a shortcoming, or is anyone’s fault.”

Every couple is different in terms of how much sex is enough for them to feel happy with it, so remember that you don’t have to meet some made-up quota of intimate evenings per week. If you are ready to get back into the groove, though, here’s how to start.

First, initiating sex after a long break comes with natural stress and pressure. If it doesn’t land with your spouse, don’t let it get you down.

“Sometimes we need a little warm-up before we get back in the saddle, so to speak. Start small. Don’t hint with memes, but act. Physical touch and flirtation are things that ignite foreplay in the mind. Kiss for a little longer than usual before you leave. Send a suggestive text during the day. Get into bed and cuddle, but without immediately reaching below the belt. You’re essentially reminding each other that you still desire each other,” Rowntree says.

It’s also totally OK to address the elephant in the room, Rowntree says. Tell your partner, “I miss being close to you. Can we make some time tonight?” This way you’re giving them an invitation and creating a little anticipation all at once.

If you go for it and your partner turns you down, don’t turn a situational no into a personal one, says Rowntree.

“When they say, ‘Honey, I’m tired,’ it becomes, ‘You don’t turn me on anymore.’ The longer you’ve been together, the more history there can be attached to that moment. If one person is usually initiating sex, or usually declining it, those long-term behavior patterns can make a huge impact.”

If there’s longstanding angst in your relationship around who initiates and how often, that in and of itself can lead to more sex droughts. It’s something to have a “frank discussion” about, Rowntree advises. During that conversation, you want to figure out how to separate “I don’t want sex right now” from “I don’t want you.”

“You want to frame your communication in a way that maintains your partner’s desirability and your interest. For instance: ‘I’m exhausted tonight, but can we cuddle?’ or, ‘Why don’t I wake you up and we can take a shower together tomorrow morning before I have to go?’ The point is, you’re declining the timing, not rejecting your partner, or giving them any ambiguity about your attraction to them.”

“Sometimes it really is the little things that turn a ‘meh, maybe’ into a spark that goes all the way. Also, please stop feeling like you need elaborate Instagram-worthy seduction schemes. There’s no reason to overcomplicate basic human desire. Put on music and pour a drink together after work. Send a flirty text before you get home. Give them a lingering kiss in the kitchen that morning. Or just say, ‘Why don’t we go to bed early tonight? I’ve missed you.’”

#8022. Are You Gonna Finish That? Why Some Dogs Always Leave Something In the Bowl

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Most dogs don't need much encouragement to finish a bowl of food, which makes it especially curious when one or two pieces of kibble are consistently left behind. It can happen meal after meal, with the same tiny piece sitting untouched at the bottom of the bowl.

There may not be one definitive reason for the habit. Instead, several explanations could account for why a dog decides that one last piece isn't worth eating, from instincts inherited from wild ancestors to simple anatomy.

One explanation goes back to the way dogs' wild ancestors had to deal with food. Unlike domestic dogs with meals that follow a predictable schedule, wild canines could never assume when, or even if, their next meal was coming.

Holding something back after eating could have provided a small reserve if the next opportunity to find food didn't go as planned. A dog leaving a single piece of kibble behind may be displaying a faint version of that old instinct, even though there is no real need to save food when another meal is readily available.

Similar behavior can be seen when dogs stash food somewhere or bury it in the yard. Wild canines would hide food after a successful hunt and return to it during leaner periods. That instinct has carried over to domestic dogs, though the original reason for it is no longer relevant.

Another possibility is that some dogs simply don't like the idea of an empty bowl.

A dog may have unconsciously associated a full bowl with having food available and, therefore, security. Leaving one piece behind means the bowl is never completely empty, avoiding that association with an empty food source.

The bowl itself could also play a role. Dogs eating from stainless steel bowls can sometimes see their reflection in the metal, which for some, may be unsettling enough that they don't want to put their face right down to the bottom of the bowl.

In that case, leaving one piece behind could have nothing to do with the food itself. The remaining kibble may simply make the bottom of the bowl, and the reflection in it, less noticeable.

The simplest explanation may also be the most obvious. A dog might leave one piece of kibble behind because it has had enough to eat.

Many dogs can regulate how much they eat and stop once they are satisfied, even when there is still a small amount of food left. If this seems to be happening, offering a slightly smaller portion at the next meal can provide an easy test.

If the bowl is consistently emptied after the portion has been reduced, the original serving size may simply have been more than the dog needed.

A vet can also help determine the appropriate amount of food based on a dog's size, age, and activity level.

There is another explanation that has nothing to do with instinct or appetite. It could simply be difficult for the dog to see the final piece.

Many dogs have a visual blind spot directly beneath their nose and snout. That means a small piece of kibble sitting at the bottom of a bowl can end up in a surprisingly awkward position.

The dog may not be deliberately refusing to eat it at all. The kibble could simply be sitting somewhere that is difficult to see.

That makes the behavior look much more deliberate than it really is. From the dog's perspective, the final piece may effectively be invisible.

One piece of kibble left in the bowl at the end of a meal is generally not something to worry about. If a dog is otherwise eating normally, the habit is likely to be one of those harmless quirks that can have a surprisingly simple explanation.

The situation is different if the amount of food being left behind gradually increases. A growing loss of appetite can sometimes point to an underlying health issue, particularly when it represents a noticeable change from the dog's usual eating habits.

Any significant change in eating habits that continues for more than a day or two is worth mentioning to a vet.

For dogs that consistently leave exactly one piece behind, though, there may be nothing mysterious or concerning happening at all. It could be an old instinct, an aversion to an empty bowl, a sign that the dog is satisfied, or simply a tiny piece of kibble hiding in a visual blind spot.

#8021. 21 Thanksgiving Table Scripts For The Relative Who Always Starts Sh*t

“I didn’t know people I knew held these types of views” is a zinger.

It happens every year but it never gets less jarring. That one drunk uncle brings up politics (and never in a thoughtful way). Your mother-in-law asks about that one sensitive subject that’s really none of her business. Your grandma comments on how much food is on your teen daughter’s plate. Whatever the topic, family gatherings have a way of bringing a bunch of people with differing opinions around one table, where they’re just comfortable enough with everyone to spew their hot takes and outdated perspectives. If you have someone like this in your family, here are some Thanksgiving table scripts to respond to that one relative who always starts sh*t.

There’s nothing worse than when that one pot-stirring family member crosses you and you immediately feel your temper flare red hot. Or you get completely flustered and fumble for words. When someone pushes a boundary of yours, take a beat before responding.

“Pause, take a breath, and press your feet into the ground to feel a bit more grounded. Give yourself permission to slow down and stay in your body so you don't feel pressured to keep answering or discussing something you're not comfortable with. You don't owe anyone at the dinner table answers you aren't comfortable giving,” says Chloë Bean, LMFT, a somatic trauma therapist in Los Angeles.

You’re not alone in feeling like the holidays are a hotbed for family conflict, experts say.

“Perhaps things start off great, but after a few rounds of seasonal cocktails, Uncle So-and-So and Grandma Such-and-Such start spouting off some out-of-pocket sh*t. This has only increased as our socio-political climate intensifies and the gap between generational understandings widens,” says Whitney Polich, LICSW, licensed clinical social worker. “Despite this happening every year, perhaps we are still a bit gobsmacked and unsure of what to say, until the drive home when the perfect clapback comes to mind.”

Whether you clap back in the moment and escalate or would rather de-escalate, practicing a few responses in your head (or even in the mirror) ahead of the gathering can help you stay grounded and protect your peace.

There are three genres of response you could go with here, says Ashley Hamm, LPC, a licensed professional counselor who specializes in anxiety and people-pleasing.

“Sometimes acting surprised or baffled is enough to throw someone off-kilter and get them off the subject. This is especially useful if someone is sharing something problematic that they might know deep down is inappropriate to share,” says Hamm.

Try these: “I’m surprised you feel comfortable sharing ideas like that.” “I have no idea what you are talking about.” “I’m surprised to hear you say that; I didn’t know people I knew held these types of views.”

Keep a few alternate subjects in the back of your mind in case you need a quick diversion — a conversational smoke bomb, if you will.

Think: “Speaking of the news, I saw a really funny story about…” “Speaking of the news, I saw a really heartwarming story about…” “I’d rather not talk about our opinions on that because I don’t get to see you very often, and I’d rather hear about what you’ve been up to personally!”

“Simply acting like you didn’t hear them is a great strategy to stay disentangled from sensitive or divisive topics. Using some of the changing topics ideas above, you can simply start a new topic, or respond to the most recent unproblematic thing someone said,” Hamm says.

For example: “Oh, Aunt Mary, you were just talking about your recipe for the green bean casserole. I’d love to hear more about where you found it.” “Hmm, not sure what to say to that. Anyways, I’ve been trying to watch more movies lately. Has anyone seen anything good?”

Bookmark ‘em for your family’s Thanksgiving and thank yourself later.

#8020. Thinking About Adopting A Cat? Here Are 4 Things To Ask Before Bringing Them Home

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

This article was created in sponsorship with Mars, which helps make content like this possible.

Pet ownership is booming, but when it comes to adoption, the biggest hurdle isnât willingness; itâs receiving the right support and guidance to adopt with confidence.

Despite there being more than one billion pets worldwide, with cat ownership specifically on the rise, new research from Mars found that 58% of pet owners have not adopted a pet from a shelter or rescue organization. Worries about the unknown, from a petâs health and behavioral history to understanding their nutritional and everyday needs, are just some of the factors that can hold people back from taking that next step.

For prospective cat owners, however, the right preparation and support can make all the difference, especially when nearly a third of respondents globally would consider it with the right support. Mars is #ClearingThePath to pet adoption by giving prospective pet parents practical, expert-backed guidance to navigate the questions that can arise before and after bringing a pet home.

Find out what medical care and health checks the shelter provides as standard. Some initial questions could be what veterinary care your cat has received (if any), including any parasite treatment, which vaccinations they have had, if they are microchipped or neutered, and whether they have any known health concerns or ongoing medications.

Once your cat is home, contact your local veterinarian to establish care for your cat. A check-up soon after adoption can help build a clearer picture of their overall health and create a plan for future preventative care. Itâs a good idea to arrange pet insurance as soon as youâve decided to adopt your cat so theyâre covered for any injuries or illnesses that may arise.

But health is only one part of understanding what your new cat needs to thrive. The SHINEâ¢ framework, developed by the Waltham Petcare Science Institute, looks at five interconnected areas of a petâs wellbeing: socialisation, health, individuality, nutrition and environment.

With that bigger picture in mind, ask the shelter about your catâs personality, temperament, energy levels, previous experiences and interactions with people, children or other pets. Understanding as much as you can about these different needs can help you consider how well your home, family, and daily routine will suit the individual cat, and how you can best support them once they come home.

Mars Research found that 71% of adopters change their petâs diet soon after adoption, but changing food immediately is not usually recommended unless a veterinarian advises it.

Ask the shelter what your cat is currently eating, how often they are fed, and whether they have any special dietary requirements. Your catâs food should be complete and balanced for their life stage, whether they are a kitten, adult, or senior. Keeping their food and feeding routine consistent initially can help make the move feel less disruptive.

If you want to change their food, wait a week or so to allow them to adjust, then do so gradually by adding a small proportion of the new food to their regular diet. On the first day, their old food should make up around three-quarters of the meal, with the new food making up the rest. Gradually increase the proportion of new food each day over a week, giving their digestive system time to get used to the new food.

If you decide to adopt a senior cat (7+ years),â¯diets designed for mature catsâ¯account for the burning of fewer calories throughout the day as well as increased palatability tailored to mature cat preferences.

Importantly, cats need diets that provide appropriate protein and essential nutrients, along with constant access to fresh water. Portion size, nutrition, and feeding style should reflect your catâs activity, age, body condition, and health; treats should remain below 10% of daily calories.

A veterinarian can help choose the most suitable diet if your cat has medical or weight concerns.

Although it can be tempting to let your new feline friend explore everywhere straight away, for many cats, a smaller and more predictable environment can feel much safer.

Consider keeping your new cat in one room before slowly giving them access to the rest of the home. During the first few days, keep windows secured and doors closed, and make sure they have everything they need close by.

Cats will seek out hiding spaces when they feel stressed, so itâs important to provide some quiet resting places while they settle in. Providing safe places to retreat to will help them navigate the unfamiliar sights, sounds, and smells around them.

Something as simple as a cardboard box placed on its side or an open cat carrier can offer a reassuring place to hide, giving them confidence to explore and interact.

Many pets need time to adjust to being alone in a new home. Start by gradually introducing short periods of separation and pairing alone time with positive experiences, such as treats, toys, or enrichment activities. Keeping departures and arrivals calm and predictable can also help build confidence and reduce stress.

If your pet shows signs of significant separation anxiety, such as destructive behavior, excessive vocalization, or distress when left alone, speak with your veterinarian or a qualified behavior professional for support and guidance.

From preparing for those first few days to supporting your petâs long-term health and nutritional wellbeing, the Mars Adoption Hub brings together trusted resources, practical advice and specialist tools designed to help you feel informed, supported and confident at every stage of the adoption journey.

#8018. 57 Uncommon Old-Fashioned Girl Names Loaded With Charm

Because you love vintage names but know way too many friends who have Avas or Olivias.

What's old is new again, and that's also true for baby girl names. Vintage names, like those from the 1920s, have been popular for a while. But since these types of names with nostalgic charm keep climbing the baby name charts, finding one that's not super popular can feel impossible. And, you know, you may not want your kid to be another Abigail in a room filled with 10 other Abigails. If that sounds like where you're at in your baby-naming journey, you'll need to dig a little deeper into the archives to find truly uncommon old-fashioned baby girl names.

Still, many new parents consider this search well worth the effort. Luckily, there's a slew of traditional names from way back when that are charming and quirky and lovely — and can easily rival the classics like Ava or Beatrice. For those genuinely looking for their baby's name to stand out, you might want to try something stunning and standalone like Elspeth or Mamie. If those tickle your fancy, keep reading for a compilation of names with an unusual quality that's elegant, edgy, and will surely stand the test of time.

Agatha is a very unique option for little girls these days, but it wasn’t always! It stayed in the top 1000 baby names from 1900 to 1945, and hasn’t been seen since. The name Agatha means “good” or “honorable,” which is such a powerful meaning for your little one.

Although it peaked in the nation’s top 100 names in 1880, Agnes fell off the charts sometime in the ‘70s. But the Greek name, which means “pure,” is poised for a comeback. The nickname Aggie, in particular,” has loads of retro charm.

From the 1880s until around the early 1930s, Alma held tight in the top 100 names for girls in the United States. It dropped pretty dramatically in the late ‘90s and early ‘00s and has settled just inside of the top 1000. A name with origins in many cultures, it means “nourishing” or “soul.”

This elegant name started strong in the 1800s, tapered off, shot to its peak in the late 1960s, and has gradually waned in popularity since. Of British and French origin, it means “noble strength.”

Latin for “venerable” or “majestic,” Augusta is grand in all the right ways. It has big great-aunt-who’s-traveled-the-world energy. Huge selling point: Gussie is an unbearably cute nickname.

Barbara is a classic in every sense of the word, and it definitely has an old-fashioned feel. The name Barbara means “foreign” or “strange,” and was most popular from the ‘20s through the ‘60s. You can use Barbie, Babs, or Barb as a cute nickname, too.

Bernie is the absolute cutest girl nickname, and the name Bernadette really sells it. This old-fashioned choice means “brave bear” or “strong,” and it was most popular in the 1920s.

An oldie but a goodie of a Greek name, Beryl means “light green semiprecious gemstone” and is perfect for the baby girl who’s the jewel of your eye.

A feminine name of Hebrew origin, Beulah means “bride.” That might make you think of how fast your daughter will grow up, but look at it like this — that’s a long way off, and it’s something to look forward to when it eventually arrives. Although this name was ranked #123 for girls in the U.S. in 1880, it’s dropped to the #6000-ish range today.

You’d think this name would have seen a bigger resurgence recently with so much love for The Golden Girls! But Blanche, a French name meaning “white” or “pure,” currently sits at #11,298 in popularity for U.S. girl names. For context, it was a top 100 name in the 1880s.

Never a wildly common name, Cicely hovered around the #5,000 mark through most of the early 1900s before dropping to its current ranking of #11,351 for girls. It means “blind of self-beauty.”

The feminine version of Claude, the name Claudette means “lame,” which isn’t all that great — but at least it’s French! It also hasn’t been popular since 1973, so you know she’ll be the only one in her preschool class.

Although Cordelia fell out of favor a little in the late ‘90s, it’s been slowly creeping back up the charts. And why not? This lovely name of Latin origin has the sweetest meaning: “heart.”

This lovely name means “steadfast,” which is exactly what you want your kid to be (except maybe at bedtime!). It feels a little prim, sure, but you could also soften it up by calling her Connie.

This beautiful name is an elaborate form of Cora. It means “little heart,” which perfectly describes your little one. It’s also forever tied to Coretta Scott King, the civil rights leader who carried her husband’s legacy forward for decades.

While the name has had some recent traction thanks to Selling Sunset’s Davina Potratz, it’s a fairly uncommon sweet name that means “beloved” — a sweet nod to your beloved bundle of joy.

From the Greek word delphís, this beautiful baby name means “dolphin” — and how cute is that? The name is also derived from Delphi, the home of an oracle in Greek mythology. It currently ranks #3643 for girl names in the U.S.

Oh goodness, imagine a sweet little baby named Dorothea! It’s just too much. This moniker means “gift of God” and has Greek origins. You can choose nicknames like Thea or Dottie, too, and hasn’t been on the popular chart since 1970.

It’s surprising that this name ranks all the way down at #15927 on the list because it’s really freaking cute! Meaning “sweet, candy,” Dulcie is related to Dulce — the name that inspired Cervantes’ Dulcinea, Don Quixote’s chosen lady.

Want your baby girl to stand strong in her voice? Consider this name, which means “well-spoken” (and happens to be the name of the tough and tenacious Effie White from Dreamgirls). Although Effie ranked #63 in the 1880s, it sits at #2120 today.

I love the simplicity of Ellen. It’s so sweet and lovely, and conjures up images of girls being badasses while also being little dollops of joy — sugar and spice and everything nice. Ellen means “torch” or “bright light” and was in the top 100 of baby girl names for literal decades. Now, it sits at #920.

A strong and sturdy name of Hebrew and Scottish origin, Elspeth means “chosen by God.” While it hasn’t made much headway outside of the U.K., it has a childish charm that might be fit for a sweet comeback.

Is Ethel not the absolute sweetest? This name just brings such joy, and its meaning is “noble.” The last time it hit the popularity charts was in the ‘70s, so I think it’s definitely time to bring back this old-fashioned cutie.

This unique name of Greek origin is perfect for your little one as it means “generous gift.” It also stems from Greek mythology, giving off some goddess vibes, too.

Like Effie, this Greek name means “well-spoken,” but it also means “sweetly speaking” — and, well, that just sounds lovely. Eulalia has a soft, earthy appeal, too, as it’s the name of a tall green grass that grows in Eastern Asia.

Faye had a good run of popularity in the ‘30s, but otherwise hasn’t come close to that same acclaim. It’s still unique now, but I suspect that the fantasy book culture has brought Faye — which means “fairy” or “belief” — back into the fold.

Don't underestimate this name that you might associate with your great-aunt! Meaning "strength of a spear," the German moniker feels a bit flinty but has a cute, much softer nickname in Gertie.

This Welsh name means “land nation,” but it has a quaint and sweet sound to it that defies its definition. And of course, there’s the Motown legend Gladys Knight, which makes it even more legendary.

Henri, Etta, Rett — so many sweet nicknames can come from the name Henrietta. It hasn’t been on the popular lists since 1968, and Henrietta also means “home ruler.”

A form of Esther, Hester means “star.” And whatever, no one cares about the Hester Prynne baggage. In fact, that kind of makes this name even cooler. A heroine who refused to be shamed into submission? Heck yeah.

An abbreviated form of Katherine, this sweet name means "pure." Naturally, it's a purr-fect name for cat lovers. It's also been the name of many famous characters, from Kitty Bennet of Pride and Prejudice to Kitty Pryde of X-Men.

In Roman mythology, Lavinia was the wife of Aeneas and the namesake of an ancient city, so this comes with a bit of historical pedigree. It’s lush and lyrical, not fussy at all, and the nickname Vinnie is so unexpectedly perfect for a little girl.

This lilting name of Hebrew and Arabic origin has beautiful (and sort of mysterious) meanings of “dark beauty” and “born at night.” If you grew up obsessed with Anna Sewell’s classic novel Black Beauty, this could be the old-fashioned girl’s name for your little one.

If you love Haunted Mansion, you undoubtedly know Madame Leota. So, while this name is pretty uncommon (#14,360 for girls’ names in the U.S.), it’s beloved in the Disney fan community. Germanic, it means “of the people.”

Loretta means “laurel,” which has such a sweet, country vibe. Retta, Lo, Etta, Rettie — there are so many cute nickname options for this old-fashioned choice. In the 1910s and ‘20s, this name was always in the top 150, and then ended up in the top 100 for pretty much all of the ‘30s.

A lovely name that means “little and womanly,” Lottie is a diminutive of the French name Charlotte. It has a “je ne sais quoi” flair that is due for a comeback... especially with the popular characters of the same name from Disney’s The Princess and the Frog and Showtime’s Yellowjackets.

I just love this one so much — it sounds like a storybook character! The name Louise means “renowned warrior,” which is pretty amazing, and while it’s gaining some traction on the popularity charts, it’s still a unique choice. (It was most popular in the 1910s.)

How sweet is Mabel? The name literally means “lovable,” and while it has gotten more popular in recent years, it’s still a unique choice for your little one. Before 2013, it hadn’t been on the popular charts since 1964.

Thanks to Hilary Duff (or Parenthood fave Mae Whitman), this darling little moniker could make a comeback, but Mae is definitely still considered old-fashioned. It’s often a diminutive of names like Margaret or Mary, but it stands on its own very well. It’s just so spunky and cute. Mae also means “maiden” or “young woman” and was in the top 100 baby girl names from 1900 to 1920.

Maude is just so punchy, I’m obsessed. This cute old-fashioned girl name hasn’t been on the popularity charts since 1950, and it means “powerful in battle.” Hell yeah, girl!

This adorable name, a shorter version of Margaret or another form of Mary, was famously chosen by Meryl Streep for her daughter Mamie Gummer. It means “pearl” and “star of the sea,” both beautiful metaphors for your new treasure.

Midge stems from the Greek word for “pearl” — but you may better recognize it as the name of the title character in Prime Video’s hit series The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel. Although the name dropped off in popularity in the ‘70s, it’s making a gradual comeback, currently ranking #2603.

This elegant English name means “gentle strength” and encapsulates both maturity and tenderness, making it a fantastic choice for the well-rounded daughter you want to raise.

Millicent just sounds vintage right off the bat, and its popularity journey truly makes that case — it hasn’t been on the lists since 1965. You can go with Millie for a cute nickname, but I truly do think Millicent just sounds so cool. It also means “strong in work.”

Who can forget Moaning Myrtle from Harry Potter? But this cute name has a richer history than that. Its origins come from the “evergreen shrub,” which was sacred to the goddess Venus as a symbol of love. So, in some ways, this name could symbolize your everlasting love for your baby girl.

OK, this might be what you call your grandmother, but it has a cute ring to it, too. The Hebrew name, which means "grace," has a uniquely modern, feminine vibe that stands out.

This gender-neutral name of Old Norse origins boasts many meanings: “wealth,” “honor,” “respect,” “man’s defender,” and “ancestor’s relic.” So, if you’re pretty sure your kid is destined to be a wild card, Ola it is! This name ranked in the top 200s during the 1880s, but today it has settled in around the #6800 mark.

Patricia feels incredibly traditional, but Patty for a little girl? Come on, we’ve got to bring it back. Patricia means “noble” and is a variant of Patrick if you like the Irish connection.

Doesn’t this just sound like it belongs to the main character of a cozy British mystery? Greek for “beloved,” it boasts a bunch of punchy nicknames like Mena, Pippa, and Pip.

OK, OK, bear with me — Prudence is extremely old-fashioned, but it also has the delightful nickname of Prue! Prudence means “wise,” “skilled,” or “intelligent,” and was extremely common during the Middle Ages. (It hasn’t been in the top 1000 baby girl names since 1948, either.)

Thanks to Dolly Parton’s immense popularity, the name Jolene has shot up the rankings in recent years. But this twangy name, which is a variant of Rae, is a much less common option (#10,919 for girl names in the U.S.) that offers the same spirit.

Calling all Ravenclaws! Harry Potter fans who call this house home will surely recognize Rowena as the first name of its founder. Outside of its HP claim to fame, the name means “famous friend” and “pure spear.” Plus, it comes with the cool nickname Ro.

Oh, Susannah! Don’t you cry for me! Whether you spell it Suzanna, Susanna, or with the traditional H at the end, this name is a classic. Susannah means “lily,” so it has a sweet, nature-related connection and a ton of cute nicknames, from Susie (or Suzie) to Suze and Anna. It was only in the top 1000 of baby girl names from 1967 to 1978, and even then, it was still one of the more unique options.

Thelma was popularized by the 1887 novel by Marie Corelli, and it means “will” in Greek. It’s peak grandma chic! And if you have two daughters, Thelma and Louise is right there. (Kidding... mostly.)

Theodora is the feminine form of Theodore, meaning “gift of God.” It’s just so cute, and Theo is a darling name for a little girl (so is Teddy, honestly!). From 1954 to 2019, it didn’t even top the charts, but it’s making a slow comeback.

Wilhelmina is just so gorgeous, and I love all of the nicknames you can pick for this one. The name also means “resolute protector,” so it feels like a strong moniker for your little gal. Bonus: It hasn’t been on the popularity charts since 1952, so you know it’s unique.

This lovely Welsh name means "blessed peace," which, sure, doesn't exactly align with everyone's favorite Winifred — the iconic red-haired witch from Hocus Pocus. But the name has a sophisticated feeling to it, and the nickname Winnie is just so delightful.

This article was originally published on July 2, 2024
